course: IB Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation SL and HL, content not shared with AA
guide: Mathematics: applications and interpretation guide, first assessment 2021 (International Baccalaureate, published February 2019), syllabus content, SL and AHL sections. Numbers, statements and recommended teaching hours were checked against the guide PDF.
about: The AI layer of the curriculum map. AI SL = the AA subtopics listed in `shared` for ai-sl plus the AI-SL subtopics here; AI HL adds the AI-AHL subtopics and the AA subtopics shared for ai-hl. A subtopic is shared only where the AI content statement matches the AA one; partly matching AI subtopics get their own AI- ID and name the AA subtopics they overlap. Topic `hours` are the AI guide's SL and AHL hours. Every AI paper allows a GDC, so every AI skill is `p2`. See curriculum/README.md.

shared.note: AI also lists a = v dv/ds and the dot notation for derivatives with respect to time; SL5.9 has no skill for these yet.

subtopics.title: Approximation, bounds, percentage error and estimation
subtopics.guide: Round to decimal places and significant figures, choosing a sensible accuracy for the data and context (for example currency). Find upper and lower bounds of rounded values, calculate percentage errors including the maximum percentage error caused by measurement rounding, and judge whether a calculated result is reasonable.

skills.name: Round to decimal places or significant figures and choose a suitable accuracy
examTypes: Write 0.004567 correct to three significant figures
Give a calculated price correct to the nearest cent, or a yen amount to the nearest whole yen
State an answer to an accuracy that matches the given measurements
Write a GDC answer correct to 2 decimal places and to 3 significant figures

methods.name: Cut at the required digit and look at the next one
methods.summary: Find the last digit to keep, then round it up if the following digit is 5 or more and leave it if it is 4 or less.

methods.name: Set the GDC to a fixed number of decimal places
methods.summary: Use the calculator's float or fix setting to display the required decimal places, then check the significant-figure count by hand.

methods.name: Choose the accuracy from the context
methods.summary: Money in euros or dollars goes to the nearest cent, many currencies such as yen to the nearest unit, and a result should not claim more precision than the measurements it came from.

misconceptions: Treating leading zeros as significant: writing 0.004567 to 3 s.f. as 0.005 (which is 3 d.p.) instead of 0.00457
Rounding in stages: 2.346 → 2.35 → 2.4 to 1 d.p., when the answer is 2.3
Dropping required trailing zeros: writing 2.9962 to 2 d.p. as 3 instead of 3.00
Giving €1234.5678 to 3 s.f. as €1230 when money should be given to the nearest cent, €1234.57

skills.name: Find the upper and lower bounds of a rounded value
examTypes: A length is 7.3 cm to one decimal place; write down its lower and upper bounds
A crowd is 3400 to two significant figures; write the inequality for the true size
Write the error interval for a mass given to the nearest 10 g

methods.name: Add and subtract half of the rounding unit
methods.summary: Rounded to 1 d.p. the unit is 0.1, so the bounds are 0.05 either side: 7.25 ≤ x < 7.35.

methods.name: Mark the rounding interval on a number line
methods.summary: Mark the neighbouring rounded values and the halfway points between them; every number between the halfway points rounds to the given value.

misconceptions: Using a whole unit instead of half: 7.3 to 1 d.p. gives 7.2 ≤ x < 7.4
Giving the upper bound as 7.34 or 7.349 instead of 7.35 with a strict inequality
Using the wrong unit for significant figures: 3400 to 2 s.f. written as 3395 ≤ x < 3405 instead of 3350 ≤ x < 3450

skills.name: Calculate the percentage error of an approximation
examTypes: A length estimated as 12 m is actually 10 m; find the percentage error
π is approximated by 22/7; find the percentage error
Find the percentage error when an answer is rounded to the nearest integer

methods.name: Use ε = |v_A − v_E| / |v_E| × 100%
methods.summary: Take the size of the difference between the approximate and exact values and divide by the exact value.

methods.name: Use the ratio of approximate to exact
methods.summary: Work out v_A / v_E, subtract 1 and take the size: 12/10 = 1.2 gives a 20% error.

misconceptions: Dividing by the approximate value: |12 − 10| / 12 = 16.7% instead of 20%
Forgetting to multiply by 100 and giving 0.2
Leaving the sign in: an estimate of 8 for 10 given as −20% instead of 20%
Rounding the exact value first (π as 3.14) so the error is computed against the wrong value

skills.name: Find the maximum percentage error in a calculated quantity from a rounded measurement
examTypes: The side of a cube is 6.4 cm to one decimal place; find the maximum percentage error in its volume
Find the largest and smallest possible areas of a field measured to the nearest metre
A speed is found from a distance and a time, both rounded; find the upper bound of the speed

methods.name: Compute the quantity at each bound
methods.summary: Find the value using the measured figure and using each bound, then use the bound further away in the percentage error formula.

methods.name: Raise the length error factor to the power of the dimension
methods.summary: A radius 2% too big makes an area 1.02² − 1 = 4.04% too big and a volume 1.02³ − 1 ≈ 6.12% too big.

methods.name: Pick bounds that push a quotient to its extreme
methods.summary: For a quotient the maximum uses the upper bound of the numerator and the lower bound of the denominator.

misconceptions: Assuming the percentage error in an area equals the error in the length: giving 2% instead of 4.04% for a circle with r = 2.5 ± 0.05
Using the lower bound only, which gives the smaller error (3.96% instead of 4.04%)
Dividing upper bound by upper bound for a maximum speed, instead of upper distance over lower time

threads.echo: A 2% error in length is a factor of 1.02; squaring for area or cubing for volume multiplies the factor, which is why the error grows.

skills.name: Estimate a result and judge whether a calculation is reasonable
examTypes: Estimate 48.7 × 3.12 ÷ 0.198 by rounding each number to one significant figure
A model predicts a negative length; explain why this answer must be rejected
Decide which of several calculator outputs is a sensible answer to a context question

methods.name: Round every number to one significant figure
Check against the context
methods.summary: Reject answers that are impossible in context: negative lengths, probabilities above 1, fractions of people, or a price in the wrong order of magnitude.

methods.name: Compare orders of magnitude
methods.summary: Write each value in standard form and combine the powers of 10 to see whether the answer is in the tens, thousands or millions.

misconceptions: Treating ÷ 0.2 as × 0.2 and estimating 50 × 3 × 0.2 = 30
Keeping a negative root from a quadratic as a length
Accepting a probability of 1.3 or an answer of 2.4 buses because the calculator gave it

subtopics.title: Amortization and annuities using technology
subtopics.guide: Use technology (the GDC finance solver or a spreadsheet) to solve loan amortization and annuity problems: repayments, number of payments, interest rate, outstanding balance and total interest. In examinations payments are at the end of each period; the annuity formula helps understanding but is not examined.

skills.name: Find the regular repayment on a loan
examTypes: A $20 000 loan at 6% per year compounded monthly is repaid over 5 years; find the monthly repayment
Find the quarterly payment needed to pay off a mortgage in 25 years
Write down the values you would enter into the finance solver

methods.name: Solve for PMT in the TVM solver
methods.summary: Enter N = 60, I% = 6, PV = 20 000, FV = 0, P/Y = C/Y = 12, and solve for PMT (about −386.66, negative because money is paid out).

methods.name: Build an amortization spreadsheet and adjust the payment
methods.summary: Each row adds a month's interest and subtracts the payment; change the payment until the balance reaches 0 at the final row.

methods.name: Use PMT = PV × i / (1 − (1 + i)^−n)
methods.summary: With i the rate per period and n the number of payments; not examined, but shows where the solver's answer comes from.

misconceptions: Entering N = 5 (years) instead of 60 payments when P/Y = 12
Entering I% = 0.5 (the monthly rate) when P/Y = 12 is already set, so the rate is divided twice
Using simple interest: 20 000 × 1.30 ÷ 60 = $433.33 instead of about $386.66
Ignoring interest: 20 000 ÷ 60 = $333.33

threads.echo: Each month the debt is multiplied by 1.005 before the payment comes off, so a loan is repeated multiplication with a subtraction at every step.

skills.name: Find the number of payments or the interest rate of a loan
examTypes: Find how many monthly payments of $500 are needed to repay a $15 000 loan
Find the annual interest rate if a $10 000 loan is repaid with 36 monthly payments of $320
Find the amount of the final, smaller payment

methods.name: Solve for N or I% in the TVM solver
methods.summary: Enter the known values with PV and PMT of opposite signs and solve for the unknown; round N up to a whole number of payments.

methods.name: Count rows in an amortization spreadsheet
methods.summary: Fill the table down until the balance drops to zero or below; the row count is the number of payments and the last row shows the final payment.

misconceptions: Rounding N down: N = 32.4 gives 32 payments, which leaves debt unpaid; 33 payments are needed
Entering PV and PMT with the same sign, so the solver returns an error or a meaningless value
Reading the solved I% as a monthly rate and multiplying it by 12

skills.name: Find the outstanding balance and split a payment into interest and principal
examTypes: Find the amount still owed after 12 payments
Find how much of the first payment is interest
Complete rows of an amortization table showing interest, payment and balance
After 3 years the borrower pays off the rest in one sum; find that sum

methods.name: Solve for FV after k payments
methods.summary: Keep PV, I% and PMT, set N to the number of payments made, and solve for FV; its size is the balance still owed.

methods.name: Fill an amortization table
methods.summary: Each row: interest = balance × periodic rate, principal repaid = payment − interest, new balance = old balance − principal repaid.

methods.name: Use the calculator's balance and interest functions
methods.summary: Functions such as bal(), ΣInt() and ΣPrn() give the balance and the total interest or principal over a range of payments.

misconceptions: Subtracting k payments from the loan: 20 000 − 12 × 386.66 ≈ $15 360 instead of about $16 464 still owed
Using the annual rate for the first month's interest: 20 000 × 0.06 = $1200 instead of $100
Assuming the interest part is the same every month: 3199.36 ÷ 60 ≈ $53.32 each time

skills.name: Find the total interest paid and compare loan options
examTypes: Find the total amount repaid and the total interest paid over the loan
Compare a 3-year loan at 7% with a 5-year loan at 5.5%: which costs less in interest?
Find how much is saved by paying an extra $50 each month

methods.name: Total repaid = N × PMT, then subtract the loan
methods.summary: Find PMT for each option on the TVM solver; interest = N × PMT − PV, for example 60 × 386.656… − 20 000 ≈ $3199.36 (using the rounded payment 386.66 gives 3199.60).

methods.name: Sum the interest column of a spreadsheet
methods.summary: Add up the interest paid in every row of each amortization table and compare the totals.

misconceptions: Giving the total repaid as the interest paid
Assuming the lower monthly payment is always cheaper overall, even though a longer term can cost more interest
Using the rounded payment in a long calculation and quoting the total to the cent as exact

skills.name: Find the future value of regular savings or the deposit needed for a target
examTypes: $200 is deposited at the end of each month at 3% compounded monthly; find the value after 10 years
Find the monthly deposit needed to save $50 000 in 15 years
Find the number of years of deposits needed to reach a target

methods.name: Use the TVM solver with PV = 0
methods.summary: Enter N = 120, I% = 3, PV = 0, PMT = −200, P/Y = C/Y = 12, and solve for FV (about $27 948).

methods.name: Sum a geometric series of deposits
methods.summary: The last deposit earns no interest and the first earns 119 months, so FV = 200(1 + 1.0025 + … + 1.0025^119) = 200(1.0025^120 − 1)/0.0025.

methods.name: Track the account in a spreadsheet
methods.summary: Each row adds a month's interest to the balance and then adds the new deposit.

misconceptions: Ignoring interest: 200 × 120 = $24 000
Treating all deposits as made at the start: 24 000 × 1.03^10 ≈ $32 254 instead of about $27 948
Entering PMT as positive with PV = 0, so FV comes out negative and is then misread

threads.echo: The account is the sum of many separate deposits, each grown for a different time: a geometric series added up by the solver.

skills.name: Find the lump sum needed for regular withdrawals, or how long a fund lasts
examTypes: Find the amount needed at retirement to withdraw $1500 a month for 20 years at 4% compounded monthly
A fund of $300 000 pays out $2000 a month; find how many full months it lasts
Find the largest monthly withdrawal a fund can support for a given time

methods.name: Use the TVM solver with FV = 0
methods.summary: Enter PMT = +1500 (received), FV = 0, N = 240, I% = 4, P/Y = C/Y = 12, and solve for PV (negative, money paid in).

methods.name: Use PV = PMT × (1 − (1 + i)^−n) / i
methods.summary: Discount every withdrawal back to today and add; not examined, but explains the solver.

misconceptions: Multiplying withdrawal by number of months: 1500 × 240 = $360 000, ignoring interest earned while the fund is drawn down
Solving for FV instead of PV, answering the wrong question
Rounding the number of full months up instead of down when asked how long full payments last

subtopics.title: Solving linear systems and polynomial equations with technology
subtopics.guide: Use technology to solve systems of linear equations in up to three unknowns and polynomial equations, using the terms zeros and roots. No particular method is required, and exam systems always have a unique solution.

skills.name: Set up and solve a system of two linear equations in context
examTypes: Adult tickets cost $a and child tickets $c; use two days' takings to find a and c
Solve a pair of simultaneous equations with the GDC
Form two equations from a word problem and interpret the solution

methods.name: Use the GDC simultaneous equation solver
methods.summary: Write each equation as ax + by = c and enter the coefficients row by row.

methods.name: Intersect the two lines
methods.summary: Rearrange each equation to y = … and find the intersection point on the GDC graph.

methods.name: Eliminate one variable
methods.summary: Scale and add or subtract the equations to remove one unknown, solve, then substitute back.

misconceptions: Entering an equation that is not in standard form, such as y = 3x + 2 entered as 3, 1, 2 (sign not changed when 3x moves across) instead of −3, 1, 2
Swapping the meaning of the unknowns when writing the answer in context
Setting up the second equation with a total count when the question gives a total cost

threads.echo: The solution of two linear equations is the point where their lines cross, so the solver and the graph give the same answer.

skills.name: Solve a system of three linear equations in three unknowns
examTypes: Solve a given system of three equations in x, y and z using technology
Three products have unknown prices; use three receipts to find each price
Write a context as three equations and solve

methods.name: Use the GDC solver for three unknowns
methods.summary: Enter each equation as ax + by + cz = d, with 0 for any missing variable.

methods.name: Write as a matrix equation and use the inverse
methods.summary: Store the coefficient matrix A and constants b, then compute A⁻¹b (links to AI-AHL1.14).

methods.name: Reduce to two equations by elimination
methods.summary: Eliminate the same variable from two pairs of equations, solve the resulting pair, then back-substitute.

misconceptions: Leaving out a zero coefficient: x + 2z = 5 entered as 1, 2, 0, 5 instead of 1, 0, 2, 5
Entering a constant on the left with the wrong sign, for example x + y − 4 = z entered with d = −4
Rounding an intermediate value and substituting it back, giving a slightly wrong final answer

skills.name: Find a quadratic or cubic model through given points
examTypes: A quadratic y = ax² + bx + c passes through three given points; find a, b and c
A ball's height is recorded at three times; find the quadratic model and use it to predict
A quadratic model passes through two given points and its height at t = 0 is known; find the model

methods.name: Substitute each point and solve the linear system
Eliminate c by subtracting equations
methods.summary: Subtract the third equation from the first: 2b = −2, so b = −1. Subtract the first from the second: 3a + b = 5, so a = 2. Then c = 4 − 2 + 1 = 3.

misconceptions: Substituting a point with x and y swapped, so (2, 9) becomes 81a + 9b + c = 2
Putting the x² coefficient in the wrong column, so a and b come out exchanged
Expecting a quadratic through only two points to be unique

threads.echo: A curve through given points and a linear system in its coefficients are the same problem written two ways.

skills.name: Find the roots of a polynomial equation with technology
examTypes: Solve x³ − 4x + 1 = 0
Find the zeros of a given quartic function
Solve 2x³ = 5x² − 3 by first writing it equal to zero

methods.name: Use the GDC polynomial root finder
methods.summary: Write the equation as f(x) = 0 and enter every coefficient in order of decreasing power, including zeros.

methods.name: Find the x-intercepts of the graph
methods.summary: Graph y = f(x) and use the zero or root tool at each crossing of the x-axis.

methods.name: Intersect the two sides of the equation
methods.summary: Graph y = 2x³ and y = 5x² − 3 and read off the x-coordinates where they meet.

misconceptions: Leaving out a zero coefficient: x³ − 4x + 1 entered as 1, −4, 1 solves x² − 4x + 1 = 0 and gives 3.73 and 0.268 instead of −2.11, 0.254 and 1.86
Entering the coefficients before moving every term to one side
Confusing a zero of f with f(0), giving the y-intercept instead of the roots

threads.echo: The roots of f(x) = 0 are the x-intercepts of y = f(x), so the polynomial solver and the graph's zero tool must agree.

skills.name: Form a polynomial equation from a context and interpret its roots
examTypes: An open box is made from a square sheet; find the cut size that gives a volume of 500 cm³
Find when a quadratic height model reaches a given height and choose the valid time
Explain why one root of the equation is rejected

methods.name: Form the equation and use the polynomial solver
methods.summary: Write the model, set it equal to the target, rearrange to = 0, solve on the GDC, then keep only roots inside the valid domain.

methods.name: Graph the model with the target line
methods.summary: Plot the model over its sensible domain with y = target; only intersections inside the domain count.

misconceptions: Keeping a negative time or length root as an answer
Keeping a cut size larger than half the sheet's side, which leaves a negative base length
Solving model = 0 when the question asks when the model equals a target value

subtopics.title: Laws of logarithms
subtopics.guide: Use the laws of logarithms for products, quotients and powers, with base 10 or e in examinations and positive arguments. Apply them to combine or expand expressions and to solve equations.

skills.name: Combine logarithms into a single logarithm
examTypes: Write 2 log 5 + log 4 as a single logarithm and evaluate it
Write ln 12 − ln 3 as a single logarithm
Express 3 ln x − ln y + ln 2 as ln of a single expression

methods.name: Apply the power law first, then product and quotient
methods.summary: Move coefficients inside as powers, then add logs as products and subtract as quotients: 2 log 5 + log 4 = log 25 + log 4 = log 100 = 2.

methods.name: Check the result numerically
methods.summary: Evaluate the original expression and the single log on the GDC; they must agree.

misconceptions: Multiplying a coefficient into the argument: 2 log 5 = log 10, giving log 40
Subtracting inside the log: ln 12 − ln 3 = ln 9 instead of ln 4
Turning a difference of logs into a quotient of logs: ln 12 − ln 3 = ln 12 / ln 3

threads.echo: The log laws rewrite an expression without changing its value, turning a sum of logs into one log of a product.

skills.name: Expand a logarithm in terms of simpler logarithms
examTypes: Express log(x³y) in terms of log x and log y
Express ln(√x / y²) in terms of ln x and ln y
Given log x = 2 and log y = 0.5, find log(x³/y)

methods.name: Split products and quotients, then bring down powers
methods.summary: log(x³/y) = log x³ − log y = 3 log x − log y = 3 × 2 − 0.5 = 5.5.

methods.name: Test with numbers
methods.summary: Pick values such as x = 100, y = √10 and evaluate both forms on the GDC to confirm the expansion.

misconceptions: Dividing the logs: log(x³/y) = 3 log x ÷ log y = 12 instead of 5.5
Applying the power to every term: log(x³y) = 3 log x + 3 log y instead of 3 log x + log y
Expanding ln(x + y) as ln x + ln y

threads.echo: Expanding a log is the reverse of combining: the same quantity in a form that shows each factor's contribution.

skills.name: Solve equations using the laws of logarithms
examTypes: Solve log x + log(x − 3) = 1
Solve ln(2x + 1) − ln x = ln 3
Use logarithms to solve 5 × 1.08^n = 12

methods.name: Combine into one log, then undo it
methods.summary: log x + log(x − 3) = 1 becomes log(x(x − 3)) = 1, so x² − 3x − 10 = 0, x = 5 (x = −2 is rejected).

methods.name: Take logs of both sides for an unknown exponent
Graph both sides and intersect
methods.summary: Plot each side as a function of x and read off the intersection, which also shows that no invalid root appears.

misconceptions: Keeping x = −2 for log x + log(x − 3) = 1, although log of a negative number is undefined
Undoing log(x(x − 3)) = 1 as x(x − 3) = 1 instead of 10
Multiplying before taking logs: treating 5 × 1.08^n = 12 as 5.4^n = 12, giving n ≈ 1.47 instead of 11.4

threads.echo: Logs and exponentials undo each other, so a log equation is solved by exponentiating and an unknown exponent by taking logs.

subtopics.title: Simplifying expressions with rational exponents
subtopics.guide: Simplify numerical and algebraic expressions with rational (fractional) exponents, using the laws of exponents and the link between fractional powers and roots, including negative fractional exponents.

skills.name: Evaluate a number raised to a rational exponent
examTypes: Find the exact value of 32^(3/5)
Evaluate 27^(−2/3)
Write 16^(3/4) as an integer

methods.name: Take the root first, then the power
methods.summary: 32^(3/5) = (⁵√32)³ = 2³ = 8; rooting first keeps the numbers small.

methods.name: Take the power first, then the root
methods.summary: 32^(3/5) = ⁵√(32³) = ⁵√32 768 = 8; valid but with larger numbers.

methods.name: Evaluate on the GDC
methods.summary: Type the exponent in brackets, 32^(3/5), to avoid the calculator reading 32^3/5.

misconceptions: Multiplying base by exponent: 32^(3/5) = 32 × 3/5 = 19.2
Inverting the fraction: 32^(5/3) instead of 32^(3/5)
Treating a negative exponent as a negative answer: 27^(−2/3) = −9 instead of 1/9
Typing 32^3/5 without brackets and getting 6553.6

threads.echo: The exponent 1/n undoes raising to the power n: x^(1/n) is the nth root.

skills.name: Multiply and divide powers with rational exponents
examTypes: Simplify (2^(1/3))^6

methods.name: Add or subtract fractional exponents
methods.summary: Same base: multiply by adding exponents, 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6; divide by subtracting, 3/4 − 1/2 = 1/4.

methods.name: Check by evaluating both forms
methods.summary: Evaluate the original and the simplified form as decimals; they must match.

misconceptions: Multiplying the exponents: 5^(1/2) × 5^(1/3) = 5^(1/6) instead of 5^(5/6)
Multiplying the bases too: 25^(5/6)
Dividing the exponents: 6^(3/4) ÷ 6^(1/2) = 6^(3/2) instead of 6^(1/4)

threads.echo: 5^(5/6), ⁶√(5⁵) and 5^(1/2) × 5^(1/3) are one number in three forms.

skills.name: Convert between roots, reciprocals and rational exponents
examTypes: Write 1/√x in the form x^n
Write 3/∛(x²) in the form a x^n
Write x^(−3/2) using a root sign

methods.name: Root index goes in the exponent's denominator
methods.summary: ⁿ√(x^m) = x^(m/n), and a reciprocal makes the exponent negative: 3/∛(x²) = 3x^(−2/3).

methods.name: Test with a value of x
methods.summary: Substitute x = 8 into both forms on the GDC to check: 3/∛64 = 0.75 and 3 × 8^(−2/3) = 0.75.

misconceptions: Writing ∛(x²) as x^(3/2) instead of x^(2/3)
Writing 1/√x as −√x or x^(−2) instead of x^(−1/2)
Moving the coefficient into the power: 3/∛(x²) written as (3x)^(−2/3)

threads.echo: Root notation and fractional exponents are two forms of the same expression; the exponent form is the one the laws (and later differentiation) work on.

skills.name: Simplify algebraic expressions with rational exponents
examTypes: Simplify (8x⁶)^(2/3)
Simplify (16a⁴b^(−2))^(1/2), giving positive exponents

methods.name: Apply the power to every factor
Substitute a test value
methods.summary: Put x = 2 into the original and the simplified form on the GDC; equal values support the simplification.

misconceptions: Not applying the power to the coefficient: (8x⁶)^(2/3) = 8x⁴
Multiplying the coefficient by the exponent: (8x⁶)^(2/3) = (16/3)x⁴
Subtracting a negative exponent wrongly: x² ÷ x^(−1) = x instead of x³

subtopics.title: Complex numbers in Cartesian form
subtopics.guide: Introduce i with i² = −1 and complex numbers z = a + bi, with real and imaginary parts, conjugate, modulus and argument. Add, subtract, multiply and divide by hand and with technology, find powers with technology, draw Argand diagrams, and solve real quadratics with negative discriminant, linking to the graph not meeting the x-axis.

skills.name: Add, subtract and multiply complex numbers in Cartesian form
examTypes: Given z = 2 + 3i and w = 1 − 2i, find z + w, z − w and zw
Write down Re(z), Im(z) and z* for a given z
Simplify i⁷
Find z z* and explain why it is real

methods.name: Use the GDC in complex mode
methods.summary: Enter both numbers using the calculator's i key and compute directly.

methods.name: Use the cycle of powers of i
methods.summary: Powers of i repeat every four: i, −1, −i, 1, so i⁷ = i³ = −i.

misconceptions: Replacing i² with +1: (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i) = −4 − i instead of 8 − i
Multiplying only matching parts: (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i) = 2 − 6i
Giving the imaginary part as 3i instead of 3
Writing the conjugate of 2 + 3i as −2 + 3i instead of 2 − 3i

skills.name: Divide complex numbers using the conjugate
examTypes: Write (3 + 4i)/(1 − 2i) in the form a + bi
Find 1/z for a given z
Find z given that z(2 + i) = 7 − i

methods.name: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator
Divide on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter the quotient in complex mode and read off a + bi.

methods.name: Write z = a + bi and equate parts
methods.summary: Multiply out (a + bi)(2 + i) = 7 − i and solve the real and imaginary equations simultaneously.

misconceptions: Dividing part by part: (3 + 4i)/(1 − 2i) = 3 − 2i
Getting (1 − 2i)(1 + 2i) = 1 − 4 = −3 instead of 5, giving (5 − 10i)/3
Multiplying only the denominator by the conjugate

skills.name: Find the modulus and argument of a complex number
examTypes: Find |z| and arg z for z = −1 + √3 i
Find the modulus of z = 3 − 4i
Find the argument of a complex number in the third quadrant

methods.name: Use |z| = √(a² + b²) and a quadrant-checked arctan
methods.summary: Find the reference angle from arctan|b/a| and place it in the correct quadrant from a sketch.

methods.name: Sketch on an Argand diagram
methods.summary: Plot the point and read the angle from the positive real axis, which prevents quadrant errors.

methods.name: Use the GDC abs and arg functions
methods.summary: The calculator returns |z| and arg z directly in the principal range.

misconceptions: Taking arctan(√3 / −1) = −π/3 straight from the calculator instead of 2π/3
Forgetting the square root: |3 − 4i| = 25 instead of 5
Including i in the modulus: √(3² + (−4i)²) = √(9 − 16)

skills.name: Find powers of complex numbers with technology
examTypes: Use technology to find (2 − 3i)⁵ in the form a + bi
Find (1 + i)⁸
Find the smallest positive n for which a given power is real

methods.name: Raise to the power on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter (2 − 3i)^5 in complex mode, using brackets around the complex number.

misconceptions: Raising each part separately: (1 + i)⁸ = 1⁸ + i⁸ = 2 instead of 16
Leaving out the brackets so only the imaginary part is raised: 2 − 3i^5 = 2 − 3i
Using the GDC in real mode and reporting a domain error as 'no answer'

threads.echo: Each multiplication by z scales the modulus by |z|, so |z^n| = |z|^n grows or shrinks geometrically.

skills.name: Represent complex numbers on an Argand diagram
examTypes: Plot z, z* and −z on an Argand diagram
Write down the complex number represented by a given point
Describe the geometric relationship between z and its conjugate

methods.name: Plot a + bi at the point (a, b)
methods.summary: The real part is the horizontal coordinate and the imaginary part the vertical coordinate.

methods.name: Use reflections and rotations
methods.summary: z* is z reflected in the real axis and −z is z rotated by 180° about the origin.

misconceptions: Plotting 2 + 3i at (3, 2) with the axes swapped
Reflecting in the imaginary axis for the conjugate, plotting −2 + 3i instead of 2 − 3i
Plotting −z as the conjugate

threads.echo: a + bi is a step of a across and b up, so an Argand diagram is a picture of complex numbers as vectors.

skills.name: Solve a real quadratic with negative discriminant and link to its graph
examTypes: Solve z² − 4z + 13 = 0
Show that a quadratic has no real roots and find its complex roots
Explain how the graph of y = x² − 4x + 13 shows the roots are not real

methods.name: Use the quadratic formula with √(−k) = i√k
Complete the square
methods.summary: (z − 2)² + 9 = 0 gives z − 2 = ±3i, so z = 2 ± 3i.

methods.name: Use the polynomial solver in complex mode
methods.summary: Set the solver to a + bi output and enter 1, −4, 13.

misconceptions: Forgetting to halve the imaginary part: 2 ± 6i instead of 2 ± 3i
Stopping at 'no solution' because b² − 4ac < 0
Writing √(−36) as −6 and getting the real roots −1 and 5

threads.echo: When the parabola never meets the x-axis there are no real roots, but the algebra still gives two complex ones.
The roots 2 ± 3i are conjugates, symmetric about the real axis, and their real part 2 is the parabola's axis of symmetry x = 2.

subtopics.title: Polar and exponential forms of complex numbers
subtopics.guide: Write complex numbers in polar form r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ and exponential form re^(iθ), and convert between these and Cartesian form by hand and with technology. Multiply, divide and raise to integer powers in polar or exponential form (finding roots is not required), add sinusoids of equal frequency using complex numbers, and interpret addition as vector addition and multiplication as a rotation with a stretch.

skills.name: Convert between Cartesian, polar and exponential forms
examTypes: Write z = 1 − i in the form re^(iθ)
Write 4e^(iπ/3) in the form a + bi
Write 5 cis(−2.1) in Cartesian form, correct to 3 significant figures

methods.name: Use r = √(a² + b²), a = r cos θ, b = r sin θ
methods.summary: 1 − i has r = √2 and θ = −π/4, so it is √2 e^(−iπ/4); 4e^(iπ/3) = 4 cos(π/3) + 4i sin(π/3) = 2 + 2√3 i.

methods.name: Use the GDC conversion functions
methods.summary: Convert with the calculator's polar and rectangular display modes, checking radians or degrees.

methods.name: Sketch the point to fix the quadrant
methods.summary: Plot the point first so that the argument has the correct sign and quadrant.

misconceptions: Losing the sign of the argument: 1 − i written as √2 e^(iπ/4)
Swapping sine and cosine: 4e^(iπ/3) = 2√3 + 2i instead of 2 + 2√3 i
Using degree mode with a radian argument, so 4 cis(π/3) evaluates as about 4.00 + 0.0731i
Giving r = 2 for 1 − i by adding the squares without the root

threads.echo: Cartesian form is best for adding and polar or exponential form for multiplying; it is the same number either way.

skills.name: Multiply and divide complex numbers in polar or exponential form
examTypes: Given z = 2e^(iπ/6) and w = 3e^(iπ/4), find zw and z/w in exponential form
Find the modulus and argument of a product
Write zw in Cartesian form

methods.name: Multiply moduli and add arguments
methods.summary: zw = 6e^(5πi/12); for a quotient divide moduli and subtract arguments: z/w = (2/3)e^(−πi/12).

methods.name: Use the laws of exponents
methods.summary: r₁e^(iα) × r₂e^(iβ) = r₁r₂e^(i(α + β)), the same rule as for any powers.

methods.name: Calculate in Cartesian form on the GDC
methods.summary: Convert both, multiply or divide on the calculator, and convert back to check.

misconceptions: Adding the moduli: 5e^(5πi/12) instead of 6e^(5πi/12)
Multiplying the arguments: π/6 × π/4 = π²/24
Subtracting the arguments in the wrong order: z/w with argument π/12 instead of −π/12

skills.name: Raise a complex number to an integer power in polar form
examTypes: Find (√3 + i)⁶
Find z⁵ in exponential form for z = 2e^(iπ/5)
Find the smallest positive integer n for which zⁿ is real

methods.name: Raise the modulus and multiply the argument
Raise to the power on the GDC
methods.summary: Compute (√3 + i)^6 directly in complex mode and compare with the polar result.

misconceptions: Raising each part separately: (√3)⁶ + i⁶ = 27 − 1 = 26 instead of −64
Multiplying the argument but not raising the modulus: 2e^(iπ) = −2
Raising the argument to the power: θ⁶ instead of 6θ

threads.echo: Each power multiplies the modulus by r again (rⁿ grows geometrically) while the argument steps on by θ.

skills.name: Add sinusoids of the same frequency using complex numbers
examTypes: Write 3 cos(5t) + 4 cos(5t + π/2) in the form A cos(5t + B)
Two AC voltage sources of the same frequency are combined; find the amplitude and phase of the total
Find the maximum total voltage of two out-of-phase signals

methods.name: Add the amplitudes as complex numbers
methods.summary: Write each term as the real part of Ae^(iα)e^(i5t); add 3e^(0i) + 4e^(iπ/2) = 3 + 4i = 5e^(0.927i), so the sum is 5 cos(5t + 0.927).

methods.name: Add the phasors as vectors
methods.summary: Draw each amplitude as a vector at its phase angle and add them tip to tail; the resultant's length and angle are A and B.

methods.name: Check with a graph
methods.summary: Graph the original sum and A cos(5t + B) on the GDC; the curves must coincide.

misconceptions: Adding the amplitudes: 7 cos(5t + …) instead of 5 cos(5t + 0.927)
Averaging the phase angles: B = π/4 instead of 0.927
Mixing degrees and radians in the phase, as when a phase of 10 means 10 radians but is entered as 10°

threads.echo: Each sinusoid becomes a vector of length A at angle α, so adding signals is vector addition.
The phase B is a horizontal translation of the cosine graph and A is a vertical stretch.

skills.name: Interpret complex addition and multiplication geometrically
examTypes: Show z + w on an Argand diagram as vector addition
Describe the transformation of the Argand plane given by multiplying by 2e^(iπ/3)
A point is rotated 90° anticlockwise about the origin; write this as a complex multiplication

methods.name: Read the stretch and rotation from re^(iθ)
methods.summary: Multiplying by re^(iθ) enlarges distances from the origin by r and rotates by θ anticlockwise; multiplying by i is a 90° rotation.

methods.name: Add tip to tail
methods.summary: z + w is the fourth vertex of the parallelogram on z and w; z − w is the vector from w to z.

methods.name: Compute and plot points
methods.summary: Calculate the product for a few points and plot them to see the rotation and stretch.

misconceptions: Thinking multiplication by 1 + i is a 45° rotation only, missing the stretch by √2
Treating multiplication by i as a reflection in the line y = x
Drawing z − w from z to w instead of from w to z

threads.echo: Adding complex numbers adds their vectors tip to tail on the Argand diagram.
Multiplying by re^(iθ) is a rotation by θ combined with an enlargement by r about the origin.

subtopics.title: Matrices: algebra, determinants, inverses and linear systems
subtopics.guide: Use matrix terms (element, row, column, order) and the algebra of matrices: equality, addition, subtraction, scalar and matrix multiplication, with the properties of multiplication and the identity and zero matrices. Find determinants and inverses by hand for 2 × 2 and with technology for larger matrices, and solve Ax = b with the inverse in contexts such as coding messages; A is always invertible in examinations.

skills.name: Use matrix terms, equality, addition, subtraction and scalar multiples
examTypes: Write down the order of a matrix and the element in row 2, column 3
Find 2A − 3B for given matrices
Given two equal matrices, find the unknowns x and y
Explain why A + B is not defined for two given matrices

methods.name: Work element by element
methods.summary: Add, subtract or scale each matching element; equal matrices have the same order and equal corresponding elements.

methods.name: Use the GDC matrix editor
methods.summary: Store A and B with their orders and evaluate the combination directly.

misconceptions: Giving the order of a 2-row, 3-column matrix as 3 × 2
Multiplying only the first row or column by the scalar
Adding matrices of different orders by padding with zeros

skills.name: Multiply matrices and use products in practical problems
examTypes: Find AB for a 2 × 3 matrix A and a 3 × 2 matrix B
A matrix of quantities sold and a matrix of prices are given; use a product to find each shop's revenue
State whether AB is defined and give its order

methods.name: Row times column
methods.summary: The element in row i, column j of AB is row i of A combined with column j of B, multiplying pairs and adding.

methods.name: Multiply on the GDC
methods.summary: Store both matrices and compute A × B; an error message means the orders are not compatible.

methods.name: Check orders first
methods.summary: (m × n)(n × p) gives m × p; the inner numbers must match, which also tells you how to arrange a context's data.

misconceptions: Multiplying element by element instead of row by column
Giving the order of a (2 × 3)(3 × 4) product as 3 × 3 instead of 2 × 4
Arranging context data so the product adds unlike quantities, such as prices of one item times quantities of another

skills.name: Use the properties of matrix multiplication, identity and zero matrices
examTypes: Show with given matrices that AB ≠ BA
Expand (A + B)² for square matrices
Simplify A I + 0 for a square matrix A
Decide whether statements about matrix products are always true

methods.name: Test with specific matrices
methods.summary: Compute AB and BA for two simple 2 × 2 matrices; one difference is enough to show multiplication is not commutative.

methods.name: Apply associativity and distributivity
methods.summary: (AB)C = A(BC) and A(B + C) = AB + AC hold, but the order of factors must be kept.

misconceptions: Expanding (A + B)² as A² + 2AB + B² instead of A² + AB + BA + B²
Assuming AB = 0 means A = 0 or B = 0
Thinking the identity matrix has every element equal to 1

skills.name: Find the determinant and inverse of a matrix
examTypes: Find the determinant and inverse of A = (2 1; 3 4) by hand
Use technology to find the inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix
Find the value of k for which a 2 × 2 matrix has no inverse

methods.name: Use det = ad − bc and swap-and-negate
Use the GDC det and inverse functions
methods.summary: Store the matrix and compute det(A) and A⁻¹; works for any n × n matrix.

methods.name: Check that AA⁻¹ = I
methods.summary: Multiply the matrix by the claimed inverse; the result must be the identity.

misconceptions: Adding instead of subtracting: det = 2 × 4 + 1 × 3 = 11
Not swapping the diagonal entries (only negating the off-diagonal): (1/5)(2 −1; −3 4)
Negating every element: (1/5)(−4 1; 3 −2)
Forgetting to divide by the determinant

threads.echo: A⁻¹ undoes the matrix A just as f⁻¹ undoes f, and a zero determinant means the process cannot be undone.

skills.name: Write a linear system as Ax = b and solve it with the inverse matrix
examTypes: Write a system of three equations in the form Ax = b
Use the inverse matrix to solve a 2 × 2 system
Set up and solve a matrix equation for the prices of three items

methods.name: Compute x = A⁻¹b
methods.summary: Store A and b and evaluate A⁻¹b on the GDC; by hand for a 2 × 2 using the formula inverse.

methods.name: Use the simultaneous equation solver to check
methods.summary: Enter the same coefficients in the equation solver; both must give the same solution.

misconceptions: Writing x = bA⁻¹, which is not defined for a column vector b
Putting the coefficients of an equation in a column of A instead of a row
Leaving a zero out of A for a missing variable, shifting the other coefficients

threads.echo: Multiplying both sides of Ax = b by A⁻¹ undoes A, like dividing both sides of ax = b by a.

skills.name: Encode and decode messages with matrices
examTypes: Encode a short word with a given 2 × 2 key matrix, using A = 1, B = 2, …
Find the decoding matrix and decode a given message
Find an unknown key matrix from a known plain text and code

methods.name: Multiply columns of letter numbers by the key
methods.summary: Group the message into column vectors, multiply each by the key matrix K to encode, and by K⁻¹ to decode.

methods.name: Solve KM = C for the key
methods.summary: When a plain-text matrix M and its code C are known, K = CM⁻¹.

misconceptions: Decoding with the key itself instead of its inverse
Multiplying a row vector on the left when the scheme uses column vectors on the right of K
Writing K = M⁻¹C instead of CM⁻¹, giving a different matrix

threads.echo: Decoding undoes encoding, so the decoding matrix must be the inverse of the key.

subtopics.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and diagonalisation of 2 × 2 matrices
subtopics.guide: Find the characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues and eigenvectors of 2 × 2 matrices by hand and with technology. Diagonalise 2 × 2 matrices with distinct real eigenvalues and use Mⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹ to find powers in applications such as population movement between two places or predator–prey models.

skills.name: Find the characteristic polynomial and eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 matrix
examTypes: Find the characteristic polynomial of M = (4 1; 2 3)
Find the eigenvalues of a given 2 × 2 matrix
Show that λ = 1 is an eigenvalue of a transition matrix

methods.name: Use λ² − (trace)λ + det = 0
methods.summary: For a 2 × 2 matrix the characteristic polynomial is λ² − (a + d)λ + (ad − bc); here trace 7 and determinant 10.

methods.name: Use technology
methods.summary: Solve the characteristic quadratic with the polynomial solver, or use an eigenvalue function where available.

misconceptions: Sign error in the trace term: λ² + 7λ + 10, giving λ = −2 and −5
Taking the diagonal entries 4 and 3 as the eigenvalues
Subtracting λ from every element instead of only the diagonal

threads.echo: The eigenvalues are the roots of a quadratic, found by factorising, the formula, or where its graph crosses the λ-axis.

skills.name: Find eigenvectors for given eigenvalues
examTypes: Find an eigenvector of M = (4 1; 2 3) for each eigenvalue
Verify that a given vector is an eigenvector and state its eigenvalue
Find the eigenvector for λ = 1 of a transition matrix

methods.name: Check Mv = λv
methods.summary: Multiply M by the vector; M(1, −2) = (2, −4) = 2(1, −2) confirms it.

methods.name: Use technology
methods.summary: Use an eigenvector function or solve the system on the GDC, then scale the result to simple integers.

misconceptions: Solving Mv = 0 instead of (M − λI)v = 0, and getting only the zero vector
Giving the zero vector as an eigenvector
Thinking a different multiple, such as (2, 2) instead of (1, 1), is a wrong answer
Matching an eigenvector to the wrong eigenvalue

threads.echo: An eigenvector is a direction the matrix does not turn: it only stretches it by the factor λ.

skills.name: Diagonalise a 2 × 2 matrix with distinct real eigenvalues
examTypes: Write M in the form PDP⁻¹, where D is diagonal
Write down P and D using given eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Verify that PDP⁻¹ = M

methods.name: Put eigenvectors as columns of P and eigenvalues on D
methods.summary: P = (1 1; 1 −2) and D = (5 0; 0 2), with each eigenvalue in the same column position as its eigenvector.

methods.name: Verify on the GDC
methods.summary: Store P and D and check that P × D × P⁻¹ returns M.

misconceptions: Writing the eigenvectors as rows of P instead of columns
Listing the eigenvalues in D in a different order from the eigenvectors in P, so PDP⁻¹ ≠ M
Writing M = P⁻¹DP with the given P

threads.echo: PDP⁻¹ is M itself, rewritten so that its stretching directions and factors can be read off.

skills.name: Use diagonalisation to find powers of a 2 × 2 matrix
examTypes: Use Mⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹ to find an expression for Mⁿ
Find M¹⁰ and check it with technology
Describe the long-term behaviour of Mⁿx as n grows

methods.name: Raise the matrix to the power on the GDC
methods.summary: Compute M^10 directly for a numerical power and compare with the formula.

methods.name: Use the largest eigenvalue for long-term behaviour
methods.summary: For large n the 5ⁿ terms dominate, so Mⁿx grows by about a factor 5 each step along the eigenvector (1, 1).

misconceptions: Raising each element to the power: Mⁿ = (4ⁿ 1ⁿ; 2ⁿ 3ⁿ)
Using P⁻¹DⁿP instead of PDⁿP⁻¹
Raising P and P⁻¹ to the power n as well as D

threads.echo: Along each eigenvector the matrix just multiplies by λ, so Mⁿ reduces to the geometric growth λⁿ.

skills.name: Apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to population and predator–prey models
examTypes: Each year 10% of town A moves to town B and 20% of town B moves to A; find the long-term population split
Use eigenvalues to find an expression for the populations after n years
A predator–prey model has a matrix with eigenvalues 1.2 and 0.6; describe the long-term behaviour

methods.name: Use the eigenvector for λ = 1
methods.summary: T = (0.9 0.2; 0.1 0.8) has eigenvalues 1 and 0.7; the λ = 1 eigenvector (2, 1) gives a long-term split of 2 : 1, so 2/3 live in town A.

methods.name: Write the state after n steps with PDⁿP⁻¹
methods.summary: x_n = PDⁿP⁻¹x₀; the 0.7ⁿ term dies away, leaving the steady state.

methods.name: Raise the matrix to a large power
methods.summary: Compute T^50 x₀ on the GDC and see the populations settle.

misconceptions: Taking the long-term split from the diagonal entries, 0.9 : 0.8
Assuming the long-term state depends on the initial split, rather than only the total
Writing the transition matrix with rows and columns swapped (rows summing to 1); its λ = 1 eigenvector (1, 1) gives a wrong 1 : 1 split instead of 2 : 1
Concluding a population dies out when the largest eigenvalue is greater than 1

threads.echo: An eigenvalue above 1 means growth and below 1 means decay along its eigenvector, exactly like the ratio of a geometric sequence.

subtopics.title: Modelling with linear, quadratic, exponential, power, cubic and sinusoidal functions
subtopics.guide: Using a family of standard functions as models of real situations: linear (including piecewise linear), quadratic (vertex, axis of symmetry, zeros and intercepts, with technology allowed for roots), exponential ka^x + c, ka^(−x) + c and ke^(rx) + c with their horizontal asymptote, direct and inverse variation ax^n (n ∈ ℤ, with the y-axis as an asymptote when n < 0), cubic, and sinusoidal a sin(bx) + d or a cos(bx) + d in degrees. For sinusoids, only amplitude a, period 360°/b and principal axis y = d are needed; converting between sin and cos is not required.

skills.name: Build and use linear and piecewise linear models
examTypes: A hire company charges a fixed deposit plus a daily rate. Write down a model for the total cost of hiring for d days
Use the conversion graph to convert 30°C to °F, and interpret its gradient
A phone plan charges nothing up to 2 GB and a fixed rate per GB after that. Find the cost of using 5 GB
Write down a piecewise linear model for the depth of a pool at a horizontal distance x m from the shallow end

methods.name: Read the rate and the starting value from the context
methods.summary: The per-unit charge is the gradient m and the fixed charge is the intercept c, so a €40 deposit plus €25 a day gives C = 25d + 40.

methods.name: Find m and c from two data points
methods.summary: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), then substitute one point into y = mx + c to find c.

methods.name: Model each interval separately
methods.summary: Write a separate linear rule for each interval, check the pieces join where the context says they should, and use the rule whose interval contains the input.

methods.name: Read values from the graph
methods.summary: Read across from the input to the line and down or across to the output; check against the equation if one is given.

misconceptions: Swaps the gradient and intercept, writing C = 40d + 25 for a €40 deposit and €25 a day, so 3 days costs €145 instead of €115
Uses the inverse conversion by mistake, computing (30 − 32)/1.8 ≈ −1.1 instead of 1.8 × 30 + 32 = 86°F
In a piecewise phone plan, charges the per-GB rate on all 5 GB instead of only the 3 GB above the free allowance
Applies one linear rule across a corner of a piecewise graph, as if the gradient never changes

threads.echo: The daily rate in C = 25d + 40 is the gradient: the cost goes up by 25 for every extra day, just like the common difference of an arithmetic sequence.

skills.name: Use a quadratic model: vertex, axis of symmetry, zeros and intercepts in context
examTypes: A ball's height is modelled by h(t) = −4.9t² + 18t + 1.2. Find the maximum height
Find the time when the ball hits the ground
Write down the equation of the axis of symmetry of the bridge's arch and interpret the y-intercept
A profit function is P(x) = −2x² + 120x − 1000. Find the number of items that gives the greatest profit

methods.name: Graph and use the maximum and zero tools
methods.summary: Graph the model with a sensible window, then read the vertex and the positive zero directly.

methods.name: Use x = −b/(2a) for the axis, then substitute
methods.summary: The vertex lies on x = −b/(2a); substitute back for the maximum or minimum value.

methods.name: Solve the quadratic on the GDC equation solver
methods.summary: Enter a, b, c to get both roots, then reject any root outside the context (such as negative time).

methods.name: Take the midpoint of the roots
methods.summary: The axis of symmetry is halfway between the two zeros, so the vertex can be found from the roots.

misconceptions: Gives the time of the maximum (t = 18/9.8 ≈ 1.84 s) when the maximum height (about 17.7 m) is asked for
Keeps the negative root of h(t) = 0 as a time when the ball lands
Uses x = b/(2a), dropping the minus sign, so the profit maximum is put at x = −30
Reads the y-intercept of h(t) as the maximum height rather than the launch height

threads.echo: The vertex of the parabola is the highest point of the flight or the best profit: the same maximum that calculus finds with f′(x) = 0.
The axis of symmetry sits halfway between the zeros, so the peak of a symmetric arch is found for free from its two feet.
Zeros of the model can be found with the formula, with the GDC solver or as x-intercepts of the graph; each checks the others.

skills.name: Use exponential growth and decay models ka^x + c and ke^(rx) + c, including the horizontal asymptote
examTypes: The temperature of a drink is T(t) = 70(0.9)^t + 20. Write down the initial temperature and the temperature it approaches
Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the model and interpret it
A population is modelled by P(t) = 1200e^(0.035t). Find the time when the population first exceeds 3000
Interpret the value 0.85 in the depreciation model V = 18 000(0.85)^t

methods.name: Substitute the input
methods.summary: Evaluate the model at the given time; at t = 0 the value is k + c, not k.

methods.name: Intersect the model with a horizontal line
methods.summary: Graph y = P(t) and y = 3000 and find the intersection to get the time a level is reached.

methods.name: Scan a GDC table
methods.summary: Tabulate the model year by year and find the first whole-number time that passes the level.

methods.name: Read the asymptote from c
methods.summary: As t grows, ka^(−t) or k(0.9)^t tends to 0, so the model levels off at y = c (for example room temperature).

misconceptions: Gives the initial temperature of T(t) = 70(0.9)^t + 20 as 70°C instead of 90°C, ignoring c
Writes the asymptote as y = 0 instead of y = c (here y = 20)
Reads V = 18 000(0.85)^t as losing 85% each year instead of keeping 85% (losing 15%)
Treats the growth as linear: 3.5% of 1200 is 42 a year, so predicts (3000 − 1200)/42 ≈ 42.9 years instead of about 26.2 years

threads.echo: Each unit of time multiplies the varying part by the same factor a, the continuous form of a geometric sequence and compound interest.
Adding c translates ka^x up by c, which is why the asymptote moves from y = 0 to y = c.

skills.name: Model direct and inverse variation with f(x) = ax^n, including the vertical asymptote when n < 0
examTypes: The pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume. Find the constant of proportionality from one reading
Intensity follows an inverse square law. Find the intensity when the distance is doubled
Write down the equations of the asymptotes of y = 12x^(−1) and explain one in context
The power from a turbine is proportional to the cube of the wind speed. Find the speed that gives a stated power

methods.name: Find a from one data point, then use the model
methods.summary: Substitute a known pair into y = ax^n to find a, then substitute the new x or solve for x.

methods.name: Reason with the scale factor
methods.summary: If x is multiplied by k then y is multiplied by k^n: doubling the distance in an inverse square law multiplies intensity by 2^(−2) = 1/4.

methods.name: Graph the model and read or intersect
methods.summary: Graph y = ax^n with a domain that fits the context and intersect with the required output.

misconceptions: For an inverse square law, halves the intensity when the distance doubles instead of quartering it
Treats 'inversely proportional' as y = a − x or y = −ax instead of y = a/x
States only y = 0 as an asymptote of y = 12/x, missing the vertical asymptote x = 0
For P = kv³, doubles v and doubles P instead of multiplying P by 8

threads.echo: In y = ax^n, multiplying x by k multiplies y by k^n: a power law works with ratios, as exponentials do, but the ratio comes from x rather than from steps in x.

skills.name: Build and use a cubic model, such as the volume of an open box
examTypes: Squares of side x cm are cut from the corners of a 30 cm by 20 cm card to make an open box. Show that the volume is V = x(30 − 2x)(20 − 2x)
State the possible values of x for the box model
Find the value of x that maximises the volume, and the maximum volume
The power output of a wind turbine is modelled by a cubic. Find the wind speed at which the output is 500 kW

methods.name: Write length × width × height from the diagram
methods.summary: Each dimension of the card loses two corner squares, so the base is (30 − 2x) by (20 − 2x) and the height is x.

methods.name: Graph on the domain and use the maximum tool
methods.summary: Graph V(x) for 0 < x < 10 only and read the local maximum, about x ≈ 3.92 and V ≈ 1056 cm³.

methods.name: Narrow down with a table
methods.summary: Tabulate V for x = 1, 2, …, 9, then refine around the largest value.

misconceptions: Takes only one corner square off each side, writing V = x(30 − x)(20 − x)
Allows 0 < x < 15, forgetting that the 20 cm side runs out first at x = 10
Picks the other turning point, x ≈ 12.7, which lies outside 0 < x < 10 and gives a negative 'volume'

threads.echo: The best box is the turning point of the cubic on its domain: the same 'find the peak' question as the vertex of a parabola.
There is no neat algebraic route at SL for the cubic's maximum, so the graph or GDC is the natural method.

skills.name: Read and use sinusoidal models a sin(bx) + d and a cos(bx) + d in degrees
examTypes: The height of a tide is h(t) = 2.5 sin(30t) + 6. Write down the amplitude, the period and the equation of the principal axis
Find the maximum and minimum height of a Ferris wheel seat from its model
A temperature model has period 12 months. Find the value of b
Find the first time after midnight when the water depth reaches 7 m

methods.name: Read a, 360°/b and d from the equation
methods.summary: Amplitude |a|, period 360°/b, principal axis y = d; maximum d + |a| and minimum d − |a|.

methods.name: Find a and d from the greatest and least values
methods.summary: a = (max − min)/2 and d = (max + min)/2; b = 360°/period.

methods.name: Graph in degree mode and intersect
methods.summary: With the GDC in degrees, intersect the model with y = 7 to find when the level is reached.

misconceptions: Gives the period of 2.5 sin(30t) + 6 as 30 instead of 360/30 = 12 hours
Gives the amplitude as a + d = 8.5 instead of 2.5
Writes the principal axis as y = 2.5 (the amplitude) instead of y = 6
Solves with the GDC in radian mode, getting meaningless times

threads.echo: a sin(bx) + d is sin x stretched vertically by a, horizontally by 1/b and moved up by d, which is why the principal axis is y = d.
The highest and lowest values come from the amplitude alone, d ± |a|, with no calculus needed.

subtopics.title: The modelling process: choose, fit, test and use a model
subtopics.guide: Following the modelling cycle with the SL2.5 (and, at HL, AHL2.9) function families: choose a suitable model and sensible domain from a context, find its parameters from initial conditions, given points or simultaneous equations solved with technology (up to three linear equations in three unknowns at SL), judge and justify the model, and use it to predict while knowing the risks of extrapolation. Fitting by regression belongs to topic 4, and SL students do not perform non-linear regression.

skills.name: Choose and justify a model type from a context, a graph or a table of data
examTypes: Which type of function would best model the depth of water in a harbour over two days? Justify your answer
The table shows the value of a car each year. Explain why an exponential model is more suitable than a linear one
Match each scatter graph to the most suitable model type
Suggest a model for a population that grows quickly at first and then levels off

methods.name: Test differences and ratios in a table
methods.summary: For equally spaced x, constant first differences suggest linear, constant second differences quadratic, and constant ratios exponential.

methods.name: Compare the shape of the plotted data
methods.summary: Look for a straight trend, a single turning point, repeating peaks, levelling to an asymptote or a vertical asymptote.

methods.name: Use features of the situation
methods.summary: Repeating cycles suggest sinusoidal, a fixed percentage change suggests exponential, a fixed rate per unit suggests linear, a limit to growth suggests an asymptote.

misconceptions: Chooses an exponential model because the values increase, when the first differences are constant (linear)
Treats constant second differences as constant ratios and picks exponential instead of quadratic
Justifies a choice only by 'it fits the points' without referring to the shape of the data or the context

threads.echo: Constant differences mean a constant rate of change, which is the signature of a linear model.
Constant ratios between equally spaced values mean repeated multiplication, the signature of an exponential model.

skills.name: Determine a reasonable domain for a model in context
examTypes: State a suitable domain for the height model of a ball from launch until it lands
Squares of side x are cut from a 24 cm card. Write down the possible values of x
A model for the number of tickets sold is valid only for whole numbers. State its domain
Explain why the model should not be used for t > 20

methods.name: Use the physical limits of the situation
methods.summary: Lengths, times and quantities must be non-negative, counts are whole numbers, and dimensions must stay positive.

methods.name: Use the zeros of the model as endpoints
methods.summary: Find where the model reaches 0 (for example the landing time of a ball) on the GDC and use it as the end of the domain.

methods.name: Limit to the range of the data
methods.summary: A model fitted to data from 2010 to 2020 is only trustworthy for inputs close to that range.

misconceptions: Gives the domain of a ball's height model as all real t, including negative times
For squares cut from a 24 cm card, gives 0 < x < 24 instead of 0 < x < 12
Uses a continuous interval for a model whose input is a count, such as the number of tickets

threads.echo: The end of the domain is often a zero of the model, found by solving algebraically or by reading the x-intercept on the GDC.

skills.name: Find the parameters of a model from initial conditions, given points or simultaneous equations
examTypes: The model P(t) = k(1.04)^t + c has P(0) = 500 and P(5) = 600. Find k and c
A quadratic model passes through three given points. Write down three equations and solve them with technology
The cost model C(n) = an + b gives C(10) = 85 and C(25) = 160. Find a and b
Use the initial temperature to find the value of k in the cooling model

methods.name: Use the value at the start
methods.summary: Substitute t = 0 to get one parameter (or a sum of parameters, such as k + c) directly.

methods.name: Set up linear equations and solve with technology
methods.summary: Substitute each point to get one equation per unknown, for example a, b, c for a quadratic, and solve the system on the GDC.

methods.name: Eliminate by hand
methods.summary: Subtract one equation from another to remove a parameter, solve for the rest, then back-substitute.

methods.name: Check against an unused point
methods.summary: Substitute a further data point into the fitted model to confirm the parameters are right.

misconceptions: From P(0) = 500 in k(1.04)^t + c, writes k = 500 and forgets c (the equation is k + c = 500)
Substitutes the coordinates the wrong way round, putting the y-value in for x
For a quadratic through (2, 9), writes 2a + 2b + c = 9 instead of 4a + 2b + c = 9, using x rather than x² as the coefficient of a

threads.echo: Each point on the curve becomes one equation; solving the system is finding the one curve of the family that passes through all the points.

skills.name: Test and reflect on a model: comment on how appropriate and reasonable it is
examTypes: Compare the model's prediction for 2018 with the actual value and comment on the model
Explain why a linear model for the cooling of a drink is not reasonable for large t
Give one limitation of the model in this context
Find the percentage error of the model's prediction and comment on its accuracy

methods.name: Compare predictions with actual data
methods.summary: Evaluate the model at data inputs, look at the differences or the percentage error, and see whether errors are small and random or growing.

methods.name: Check the long-run behaviour
methods.summary: Ask what the model does as the input grows: a negative temperature, an unlimited population or a negative price signals that the model fails there.

methods.name: Check the model against the real situation
methods.summary: Look for assumptions that the context breaks, such as constant growth with limited resources, or a whole-number quantity modelled as continuous.

misconceptions: Concludes the model is good because it passes exactly through the two points used to fit it
Calls a model unsuitable because it is not exact for one point, without considering the overall pattern or the size of the error
Divides by the model's value instead of the actual value in the percentage error, getting a slightly wrong percentage

threads.echo: Plotting the model over the data makes a mismatch visible that a single substituted value can hide.

skills.name: Use a model to read values, interpret parameters and make predictions, recognising the risk of extrapolation
examTypes: Use the model to predict the population in 2030 and comment on the reliability of your prediction
Interpret the value of c in the context of the model
Use the model to find when the value first falls below €5000
Explain why a prediction for x = 100 is less reliable than one for x = 12

methods.name: Substitute into the model
methods.summary: Evaluate the model at the required input, converting a calendar year to the model's time variable first.

methods.name: Solve for the input on the GDC
methods.summary: Intersect the model with a horizontal line or use the solver to find when a level is reached.

methods.name: Decide whether the input is inside the data range
methods.summary: Predictions inside the data range (interpolation) are more reliable than those far outside it (extrapolation).

misconceptions: Substitutes the year 2030 for t when t is years since 2010 (t = 20)
Trusts an extrapolation far outside the data because the model fitted the data well
Interprets a parameter in the wrong units, for example reading the daily rate as the total cost

threads.echo: Finding the time a level is reached runs the model backwards: given the output, recover the input.

subtopics.title: Composite and inverse functions in context
subtopics.guide: Composite functions (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) set in context, and inverse functions: finding f⁻¹, using f ∘ f⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ f = identity, and restricting a domain (for example to one side of a quadratic's vertex) so an inverse exists.

skills.name: Form, evaluate and interpret a composite function in context
examTypes: A factory makes n(t) items in t hours and the cost of n items is C(n). Find (C ∘ n)(8) and interpret it
Write down an expression for C(n(t)) and state what it represents
A currency conversion is followed by a fixed fee. Express the total as a composite function
Given f(x) and g(x), find (f ∘ g)(x) and (g ∘ f)(x) and comment on which makes sense in context

methods.name: Evaluate the inner function first
methods.summary: For (C ∘ n)(8), find n(8), then put that number into C.

methods.name: Substitute the whole inner expression
methods.summary: Replace every x in the outer function by g(x) and simplify, so the composite can be used for any input.

methods.name: Follow the units through the chain
methods.summary: Hours go into n to give items, items go into C to give cost; the order that makes the units match is the meaningful composite.

methods.name: Define both functions on the GDC
methods.summary: Store f and g as Y1 and Y2 and evaluate Y1(Y2(8)) to check a hand calculation.

misconceptions: Applies the outer function first, computing n(C(8)) instead of C(n(8))
Multiplies C(8) × n(8) instead of composing
Replaces only one x in the outer function by g(x), leaving the others as x
Assumes f ∘ g = g ∘ f in every context

threads.echo: A composite is a chain of processes; undoing it means undoing the last step first, so (f ∘ g)⁻¹ = g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹.

skills.name: Find an inverse function and interpret it in context
examTypes: The conversion F(C) = 1.8C + 32 changes Celsius to Fahrenheit. Find F⁻¹ and use it to convert 50°F
Find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 5(x − 2)³ + 1
Find the inverse of a taxi fare model and state what it calculates
Find f⁻¹(10) without finding f⁻¹(x)

methods.name: Swap x and y, then make y the subject
methods.summary: Write x = 1.8y + 32 and rearrange to y = (x − 32)/1.8.

methods.name: Undo the operations in reverse order
methods.summary: F multiplies by 1.8 then adds 32, so F⁻¹ subtracts 32 then divides by 1.8.

methods.name: Solve f(x) = k on the GDC for a single value
methods.summary: f⁻¹(10) is the x with f(x) = 10, which can be found by intersecting y = f(x) with y = 10.

misconceptions: Writes F⁻¹(x) = 1/(1.8x + 32), treating the inverse as a reciprocal
Undoes the steps in the original order, giving x/1.8 − 32, so 50°F becomes −4.2°C instead of 10°C
Evaluates f(10) when f⁻¹(10) is asked for

threads.echo: F⁻¹ undoes F: Fahrenheit back to Celsius is the same 'undo' as ln undoing e^x.

skills.name: Restrict a domain so that an inverse exists, and find the domain and range of the inverse
examTypes: Explain why f(x) = (x + 1)² + 4 has no inverse on ℝ
State the largest domain of the form x ≥ k for which f has an inverse, and find f⁻¹(x)
Write down the domain and range of f⁻¹
A model is only invertible for part of its domain. State which part makes sense in the context

methods.name: Restrict at the turning point
methods.summary: A quadratic is one-to-one on either side of its vertex, so (x + 1)² + 4 is invertible for x ≥ −1 or for x ≤ −1.

methods.name: Use the horizontal line test on the graph
methods.summary: If some horizontal line meets the graph twice the function is not one-to-one; cut the domain until every line meets it at most once.

methods.name: Swap domain and range
methods.summary: The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f: here f⁻¹(x) = −1 + √(x − 4) for x ≥ 4.

misconceptions: Gives the domain of f⁻¹ as x ≥ −1 (the domain of f) instead of x ≥ 4 (the range of f)
Keeps the ± and writes f⁻¹(x) = −1 ± √(x − 4), which is not a function
Restricts the domain at the y-intercept (x ≥ 0) instead of at the vertex x = −1, so the inverse misses part of the branch
Picks the negative square root when the domain was restricted to x ≥ −1

threads.echo: Like x² needing x ≥ 0 before √x can undo it, a model must be one-to-one before it can be undone.
The two halves of a parabola mirror each other in the axis of symmetry, which is why the cut must be made at the vertex.

skills.name: Use f ∘ f⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ f = x and the reflection of a graph in y = x
examTypes: Write down (f ∘ f⁻¹)(7)
Given f⁻¹(a) = 3, find a
Sketch the graph of f⁻¹ on the same axes as f
Verify that g is the inverse of f by finding (f ∘ g)(x)

methods.name: Use the identity property directly
methods.summary: Composing a function with its inverse returns the input, so (f ∘ f⁻¹)(7) = 7 with no working.

methods.name: Compose and simplify to x
methods.summary: Substitute g(x) into f and simplify; if the result is x (and g ∘ f also gives x), then g = f⁻¹.

methods.name: Reflect the graph in y = x
methods.summary: Swap the coordinates of key points and asymptotes: (2, 5) on f becomes (5, 2) on f⁻¹.

methods.name: Draw the inverse on the GDC
methods.summary: Use the GDC's draw-inverse feature or graph x = f(y) parametrically to check a sketch.

misconceptions: Thinks (f ∘ f⁻¹)(x) = 1 rather than x
From f⁻¹(a) = 3, writes a = f⁻¹(3) instead of a = f(3)
Reflects the graph in the x-axis or y-axis instead of in the line y = x

threads.echo: Doing then undoing leaves you where you started; on a graph, undoing is a reflection in y = x.
The graph of f⁻¹ is a reflection of f, so every point and asymptote swaps its coordinates.

subtopics.title: Further models: half-life, logarithmic, sinusoidal, logistic and piecewise
subtopics.guide: Extending the SL model families with half-life from exponential models, natural logarithmic models f(x) = a + b ln x, sinusoidal models a sin(b(x − c)) + d in radians (period 2π/b, with c a phase shift), logistic models L/(1 + Ce^(−kx)) with carrying capacity L, and piecewise models, including finding a parameter that makes the pieces join. Students may also meet unfamiliar models defined in a question; the formal definition of continuity is not required.

skills.name: Find and use half-life with exponential decay models
examTypes: The mass of a sample is M(t) = 80e^(−0.12t). Find the half-life
A substance has a half-life of 5.3 years. Find the value of k in N = N₀e^(−kt)
A drug's concentration falls by 8% each hour. Find how long it takes to halve
Find the time taken for the activity to fall to 10% of its initial value

methods.name: Set the model equal to half and take logs
methods.summary: e^(−kt) = 1/2 gives t = ln 2 / k; for a base form (0.92)^t = 0.5 gives t = ln 0.5 / ln 0.92 ≈ 8.31 hours.

methods.name: Intersect with half the initial value
methods.summary: Graph the model and y = M(0)/2 and read the time at the intersection.

methods.name: Use N = N₀(1/2)^(t/T)
methods.summary: Writing the model with the half-life T in the exponent lets you read T directly or convert to k with k = ln 2 / T.

misconceptions: Uses T = 1/(2k), getting about 4.17 years for k = 0.12 instead of ln 2 / 0.12 ≈ 5.78
Thinks halving takes 50/8 = 6.25 hours for an 8% hourly decrease, treating the decay as linear
Solves 80e^(−0.12t) = 0.5 instead of 80e^(−0.12t) = 40, setting the amount to 0.5 rather than half the initial amount
Thinks the half-life depends on the starting amount

threads.echo: Every half-life multiplies the amount by 1/2 again, so the half-life is the same no matter how much you start with.
Logarithms undo the exponential to bring the time down from the exponent.

skills.name: Use natural logarithmic models f(x) = a + b ln x
examTypes: A model is f(x) = a + b ln x with f(2) = 10 and f(8) = 16. Find a and b
Use the model to find the value of x for which f(x) = 20
Interpret the value of a in the context of the model
Explain why the model cannot be used at x = 0

methods.name: Substitute two points and solve the linear system
methods.summary: a + b ln 2 = 10 and a + b ln 8 = 16 are linear in a and b; solving gives b = 6/ln 4 ≈ 4.33 and a = 7.

methods.name: Subtract and use the log laws
methods.summary: Subtracting gives b(ln 8 − ln 2) = b ln 4 = 6, then substitute back for a.

methods.name: Solve for x by exponentiating
methods.summary: From a + b ln x = k, ln x = (k − a)/b, so x = e^((k − a)/b).

methods.name: Intersect the model with the target value
methods.summary: Graph the model for x > 0 and intersect with y = k.

misconceptions: Takes a as f(0), when ln 0 is undefined; a is the value at x = 1
Uses log base 10 instead of ln when substituting, getting different values of a and b
Solves ln x = k as x = k/e or x = ke instead of x = e^k

threads.echo: To get x out of a + b ln x, undo the ln with e^( ), just as ln undoes e^x.
In a + b ln x, multiplying x by the same factor always adds the same amount b ln(factor): growth by equal steps for equal ratios.

skills.name: Find and use sinusoidal models a sin(b(x − c)) + d in radians, including the phase shift
examTypes: High tide is 11 m at 05:00 and the next low tide is 3 m at 11:00. Find a, b, c and d for d(t) = a sin(b(t − c)) + d
Write down the period of h(t) = 4 sin(0.5(t − 1)) + 12 and the phase shift
Find the times in the first 24 hours when the depth is above 9 m
Explain what the value of c represents in this model

methods.name: Use maximum, minimum and period
methods.summary: a = (11 − 3)/2 = 4, d = (11 + 3)/2 = 7, max to min is half a period so the period is 12 h and b = 2π/12 = π/6.

methods.name: Place a point of the sine wave to find c
methods.summary: sin reaches its maximum a quarter-period after crossing the principal axis upwards, so a maximum at t = 5 with period 12 gives c = 5 − 3 = 2.

methods.name: Intersect with the level in radian mode
methods.summary: Graph the model and y = 9 in radians and read every intersection in the interval to find when the depth is above 9.

misconceptions: Takes the time from maximum to minimum (6 h) as the period, giving b = π/3 instead of π/6
Uses 360°/b or works in degree mode when the model is in radians
Puts the maximum at t = c, giving c = 5 instead of 2, as if the model were a cosine
Gives only the first interval when the depth is above 9 m, missing the next cycle

threads.echo: The phase shift c is a horizontal translation: replacing x with x − c moves the whole wave right by c.
a sin(b(x − c)) + d places the stretched wave by the translation vector (c, d).
The highest and lowest tides are d ± |a|, read off the model without differentiating.

skills.name: Use logistic models L/(1 + Ce^(−kx)), including the carrying capacity
examTypes: A population of fish is modelled by P(t) = 500/(1 + 24e^(−0.3t)). Write down the initial population and the carrying capacity
Find the time when the population reaches 400
Given the initial value and the carrying capacity, find C
Explain why a logistic model is more suitable than an exponential model for bacteria in a petri dish

methods.name: Read L and the initial value from the formula
methods.summary: As t grows, e^(−kt) → 0 so P → L (the asymptote y = L); at t = 0, P = L/(1 + C), here 500/25 = 20.

methods.name: Find C from the initial value
methods.summary: Rearranging P(0) = L/(1 + C) gives C = L/P(0) − 1.

methods.name: Intersect with a target level
methods.summary: Graph the model and y = 400 and read the time; P = 400 at t ≈ 15.2.

misconceptions: Gives the initial population as 500 (the carrying capacity) instead of 500/25 = 20
Finds C as L − P(0) = 480 instead of L/P(0) − 1 = 24
Thinks the population will eventually pass the carrying capacity if t is large enough
Gives the carrying capacity as L/(1 + C)

threads.echo: Early on the logistic model grows almost exponentially, but the limit L slows the repeated multiplication to a halt.
Finding when a level is reached means undoing the model step by step, ending with a logarithm to undo e^(−kt).

skills.name: Interpret, evaluate and build piecewise models from a context
examTypes: A taxi charges a fixed fee for the first 2 km and a rate per km after that. Write down a piecewise model for the fare
Use the income tax model to find the tax paid on an income of €48 000
Sketch the graph of the piecewise model and interpret the change in gradient
A parachutist's speed is given by two formulas, before and after the chute opens. Find the speed at a given time

methods.name: Choose the piece whose interval contains the input
methods.summary: Check which interval the input lies in, including the endpoint convention (< or ≤), and evaluate only that rule.

methods.name: Work band by band
methods.summary: For tax or postage, apply each rate only to the part of the amount in its band and add the parts.

methods.name: Read the graph
methods.summary: Read the output from the correct section of the graph, noticing closed and open endpoints and changes of gradient.

misconceptions: Applies the top tax rate to the whole income instead of only the part above the threshold
Uses the wrong piece at a boundary, ignoring whether the inequality is < or ≤
Starts the second piece of a taxi fare from 0 km rather than from the end of the first piece, double-charging the first 2 km

threads.echo: Each piece of a piecewise linear model has its own rate; the corners are where the rate of change switches.

skills.name: Find a parameter that makes a piecewise model continuous
examTypes: Find the value of a so that f(x) = 3x + 1 for 0 ≤ x < 4 and f(x) = ax² − 3 for x ≥ 4 is continuous
A water tank model switches formula at t = 10. Find k so that there is no jump in the volume
