The scatter diagram shows a curved increasing pattern. Which coefficient should be used? Justify
The data are given only as rankings. State which coefficient can be calculated

methods.name: Look at the shape of the scatter
methods.summary: A roughly straight pattern suits Pearson's r; a curved pattern that only rises (or only falls) suits rs, because rs tests for any monotonic relationship.

methods.name: Check what kind of data you have
methods.summary: Data that exist only as ranks or orderings (judges' placings, preferences) call for rs; measured data with a linear trend can use r.

misconceptions: Using Pearson's r for a clearly curved but increasing pattern and concluding the association is weak
Thinking rs and r always give the same value, so the choice does not matter
Thinking rs detects any relationship, including a U-shape (a U-shape is not monotonic, so rs can be close to 0)

skills.name: Describe the effect of an outlier on r and on rs
examTypes: An extra data point is added. Find the new values of r and rs and comment
Explain why rs changes less than r when the outlier is included
Which coefficient would you report for these data? Give a reason

methods.name: Recalculate with and without the point
methods.summary: Find r and rs on the GDC with the outlier included and excluded, then compare how much each changes.

methods.name: Reason from ranks
methods.summary: An outlier can only take the top or bottom rank, however extreme its value, so it moves rs by a limited amount; r uses the actual distances, so one far-away point can change it a lot.

misconceptions: Thinking Spearman's rs ignores outliers completely, so it cannot change at all
Thinking an outlier always makes r smaller (an outlier in line with the trend can increase r)
Deleting an outlier from one coefficient's calculation but not the other's before comparing them

subtopics.title: Hypothesis testing: χ² tests and the t-test
subtopics.guide: Writing null and alternative hypotheses and reaching conclusions with significance levels and p-values; χ² tests for independence (contingency tables up to 4 × 4, degrees of freedom, critical values) and goodness of fit, using expected and observed frequencies; the pooled two-sample t-test for unpaired samples from normal populations, one- or two-tailed. Exam tests are upper-tail at 1%, 5% or 10%, the statistic and p-value come from technology, and expected frequencies exceed 5.

skills.name: Write H₀ and H₁, and make a decision from a p-value or critical value
examTypes: State the null and alternative hypotheses for this test
The p-value is 0.032. State, with a reason, the conclusion at the 5% significance level
The χ² statistic is 9.21 and the critical value is 7.815. Write a conclusion in context

methods.name: Compare p with the significance level
methods.summary: If p < α, reject H₀; if p > α, do not reject H₀. Then say what that means for the variables or populations in the question.

methods.name: Compare the statistic with the critical value
methods.summary: If the test statistic is greater than the given critical value it lies in the rejection region, so reject H₀; otherwise do not reject H₀.

misconceptions: Rejecting H₀ when p = 0.032 at the 1% level because p is 'small'
Writing 'accept H₀' or 'H₀ is proved true' instead of 'there is insufficient evidence to reject H₀'
Putting the claim being tested into H₀ and the 'no effect' statement into H₁
Comparing the p-value with the critical value rather than with the significance level

skills.name: Calculate expected frequencies for a χ² test
examTypes: Show that the expected frequency for left-handed adults is 10
Complete the table of expected frequencies
A die is rolled 120 times. Write down the expected frequency for each score if the die is fair

methods.name: Row total × column total ÷ grand total
methods.summary: For a contingency table, each expected frequency is (row total × column total) ÷ grand total, for example 40 × 30 ÷ 120 = 10.

methods.name: Total × hypothesised probability
methods.summary: For goodness of fit, multiply the total number of observations by the probability of each category under H₀, so a fair die rolled 120 times gives 20 for each score.

methods.name: Read the expected matrix from the GDC
methods.summary: After running the χ² test on the observed matrix, the GDC stores the expected frequencies in a matrix that can be displayed.

methods.name: Fill the rest from the totals
methods.summary: Expected frequencies have the same row and column totals as the observed table, so once some cells are known the others follow by subtraction.

misconceptions: Multiplying row total by column total and forgetting to divide by the grand total (1200 instead of 10)
Dividing the row total by the grand total and stopping (0.333 instead of 10)
Giving expected frequencies rounded to whole numbers because 'you cannot have part of a person'

threads.echo: Expected frequencies share the row and column totals of the observed table, so filling one cell gives others for free by subtraction.

skills.name: Carry out a χ² test for independence on a contingency table
examTypes: Test at the 5% level whether choice of sport is independent of year group
Write down the number of degrees of freedom for this test
Find the χ² statistic and the p-value, and state the conclusion

methods.name: χ² test on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter the observed frequencies as a matrix (without totals), run the χ² two-way test and read the statistic, p-value and degrees of freedom.

methods.name: Σ(O − E)²/E by hand
methods.summary: Find each expected frequency, add (O − E)²/E over all cells to get the statistic, and compare it with the given critical value with (r − 1)(c − 1) degrees of freedom.

misconceptions: Using degrees of freedom r × c − 1 = 11 for a 3 × 4 table instead of (3 − 1)(4 − 1) = 6
Including the row and column totals in the GDC matrix
Writing H₀ as 'the variables are dependent'
Concluding that one variable causes the other after rejecting independence

skills.name: Carry out a χ² goodness of fit test
examTypes: Test at the 10% level whether the die is fair
A seed company claims its colours come in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Test this claim
Write down the degrees of freedom and find the p-value

methods.name: χ² GOF test on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter observed frequencies in one list and expected in another, set degrees of freedom to (number of categories − 1) and read the statistic and p-value.

methods.name: Σ(O − E)²/E against a critical value
methods.summary: Work out (O − E)²/E for each category, add them, and compare the total with the given critical value.

misconceptions: Entering the hypothesised proportions (0.5, 0.333, 0.167) as the expected list instead of the expected frequencies
Using the number of categories as the degrees of freedom (6 for a die instead of 5)
Entering the expected list as 'observed', which gives a different χ² value

skills.name: Compare two population means with a pooled two-sample t-test
examTypes: Test at the 5% level whether the mean time for group A is greater than for group B
Explain whether a one-tailed or a two-tailed test is appropriate
State an assumption needed for the t-test to be valid

methods.name: 2-SampTTest with pooling on
methods.summary: Enter the two samples (or their summary statistics), choose the alternative μ₁ > μ₂, μ₁ < μ₂ or μ₁ ≠ μ₂, set pooled to yes, and read the p-value.

methods.name: Read the tail from the claim
methods.summary: Words like 'greater', 'faster' or 'improves' give a one-tailed H₁; 'different' or 'changed' gives a two-tailed H₁.

misconceptions: Choosing a two-tailed test for a 'greater than' claim, which doubles the p-value
Leaving pooled set to 'no', which gives a slightly different p-value from the expected answer
Writing hypotheses about the sample means x̄₁ and x̄₂ instead of the population means μ₁ and μ₂
Forgetting that both populations must be normally distributed for the test to be valid

subtopics.title: Designing data collection; reliability and validity
subtopics.guide: Designing valid data collection, including surveys and questionnaires with structured, unbiased and precise questions; choosing relevant variables and data to analyse; grouping numerical data into categories for a χ² test so that expected frequencies exceed 5, and reducing the degrees of freedom for each parameter estimated from the data; the difference between reliability and validity, with test-retest and parallel-forms reliability, and content and criterion-related validity.

skills.name: Identify bias or imprecision in a survey question and improve it
examTypes: Explain why this question may produce biased results
Suggest an improved version of the question
Explain one disadvantage of the answer choices offered

methods.name: Check against a list of flaws
methods.summary: Look for leading wording, personal or sensitive content, vague terms (such as 'often'), overlapping or missing answer choices, and open answers that cannot be compared.

methods.name: Rewrite as a structured question
methods.summary: Use neutral wording and a fixed set of non-overlapping answer choices that cover every possibility, such as 0, 1–2, 3–5, 6 or more.

misconceptions: Accepting answer bands such as 0–5, 5–10 that overlap at 5
Thinking an open, unstructured question is always better because it gives more detail (the answers cannot be compared or analysed easily)
Thinking a large sample removes the bias caused by a leading question

skills.name: Select relevant variables and appropriate data for an investigation
examTypes: From the variables in the data set, choose two that could test the claim, and justify your choice
Explain why this data set is not appropriate for answering the question
Suggest a variable that should be recorded to make the comparison fair

methods.name: Match the variables to the claim
methods.summary: Identify exactly what the claim compares or relates, and pick the variables that measure those things directly, ignoring the rest.

methods.name: Check the data are suitable
methods.summary: Ask whether the data cover the right population and time, are recorded consistently, and are numerical or categorical as the intended test requires.

misconceptions: Choosing a variable that is easy to measure rather than one that answers the question
Using data from a different population (for example adults) to make a claim about another (teenagers)
Including every available variable, thinking more variables always gives a better analysis

skills.name: Group numerical data into χ² categories and justify the grouping
examTypes: Explain why the last two groups must be combined before the test
Group the data into categories suitable for a χ² goodness of fit test
Justify your choice of categories

methods.name: Merge cells with expected ≤ 5
methods.summary: Compute the expected frequencies first, then combine a category whose expected frequency is 5 or less with a neighbouring one, adding both observed and expected values.

methods.name: Plan class boundaries in advance
methods.summary: Choose class boundaries so that every class is expected to hold more than 5 values, often using wider classes in the tails where data are sparse.

misconceptions: Merging categories because the observed frequency is small rather than the expected frequency
Combining the expected frequencies but leaving the observed frequencies separate
Forgetting that merging categories reduces the degrees of freedom

skills.name: Choose the degrees of freedom when parameters are estimated from the data
examTypes: The mean of the Poisson model was estimated from the sample. Write down the degrees of freedom
Explain why the degrees of freedom are 3 and not 5
Test whether a normal distribution, with mean and standard deviation estimated from the data, is a good fit

methods.name: Categories − 1 − parameters estimated
methods.summary: Start with the number of categories after merging, subtract 1 for the fixed total and 1 more for each parameter estimated from the data: Poisson with λ estimated loses 2, normal with μ and σ estimated loses 3.

methods.name: Set df by hand on the GDC
methods.summary: The GDC goodness of fit test does not know which parameters were estimated, so type the reduced degrees of freedom into the df field before calculating.

misconceptions: Using categories − 1 = 5 for six classes fitted by a normal model with μ and σ estimated (correct is 3)
Subtracting a degree of freedom for a parameter that was given in the claim, not estimated from the data
Counting the categories before merging small cells

skills.name: Distinguish reliability from validity
examTypes: Explain the difference between reliability and validity
A scale always reads 2 kg too heavy. Is it reliable, valid, both or neither?
State whether this description refers to reliability or to validity

methods.name: Consistent versus measuring the right thing
methods.summary: Reliable means the method gives consistent results when repeated; valid means it actually measures what it claims to measure.

methods.name: Target diagram
methods.summary: Shots clustered together but off centre are reliable but not valid; shots centred on the bullseye and clustered are both.

misconceptions: Thinking a reliable test must also be valid (a scale that is always 2 kg too heavy is reliable but not valid)
Using 'reliable' to mean 'accurate'
Thinking validity can be shown by repeating the test and getting the same scores

skills.name: Choose and apply a reliability or validity test
examTypes: Name a suitable test of reliability for this questionnaire and describe how it is carried out
The same students sat the test twice. Use the scores to comment on the test's reliability
Explain how criterion-related validity could be checked for a new fitness test

methods.name: Correlate two sets of scores
methods.summary: For test-retest (same test, same group, two occasions) or parallel forms (two equivalent versions), find Pearson's r between the paired scores; a strong positive r suggests the test is reliable.

methods.name: Compare with an established criterion
methods.summary: Criterion-related validity compares results with a trusted measure or later outcome, often through correlation; content validity asks whether the test covers the full range of what it should measure, usually judged by experts.

misconceptions: Calling test-retest a validity test
Calling content validity a numerical calculation, when it is a judgement about coverage
Treating a strong negative r between two sittings as evidence of reliability

subtopics.title: Non-linear regression and the coefficient of determination
subtopics.guide: Fitting least squares regression curves with technology: linear, quadratic, cubic, exponential, power and sine models; the sum of square residuals SSres as a measure of fit; the coefficient of determination R² as the proportion of variation in y explained by the model, with R² = r² for linear models. R² alone is not a reliable way to choose between models; the formula R² = 1 − SSres/SStot is not examined.

skills.name: Find a non-linear regression model with technology and use it to predict
examTypes: Find the equation of the exponential regression model y = abˣ
Find the power model y = axᵇ for the data and use it to estimate y when x = 7
Find a sine regression model for the monthly temperatures

methods.name: Regression menu on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter x and y in two lists and choose QuadReg, CubicReg, ExpReg, PwrReg or SinReg, then write the parameters to 3 significant figures, but substitute the unrounded values stored by the GDC to predict.

methods.name: Linearise with logarithms
methods.summary: For y = abˣ, a linear regression of ln y on x gives ln b as gradient and ln a as intercept; for y = axᵇ, regress ln y on ln x. Note the GDC exponential and power fits use this route, so they minimise residuals in ln y.

misconceptions: Choosing ExpReg when the model asked for is y = axᵇ (power), giving the wrong equation
Swapping the lists so that x is regressed on y
Using rounded parameters for a prediction and losing accuracy at large x

threads.echo: An exponential model y = abˣ says y is multiplied by b for each unit step in x, the same idea as a geometric sequence with common ratio b.

skills.name: Choose a suitable type of regression model from the data and context
examTypes: Which type of model is most appropriate for the scatter diagram? Justify
Explain why a sine model suits the data
Explain why a quadratic model is unrealistic for large values of t

methods.name: Match the scatter shape
methods.summary: Repeating peaks suggest sine; one turning point suggests quadratic; growth by a constant factor or decay towards an asymptote suggests exponential; a curve through the origin suggests power.

methods.name: Check long-run behaviour in context
methods.summary: Ask what the model does outside the data: a quadratic eventually turns back, an exponential decay never goes below its asymptote, and a cubic can go negative where values must be positive.

misconceptions: Choosing the model with the largest R² even when it predicts impossible values in context
Choosing a quadratic for data that level off towards a limit, so the model eventually turns round and decreases
Thinking every curved scatter is quadratic

threads.echo: A sine regression model a·sin(b(x − c)) + d reads like a transformed sin x: amplitude a, period 2π/b, horizontal shift c and vertical shift d.

skills.name: Calculate and compare the sum of square residuals
examTypes: Find the residual for the point (3, 6) using the model
Calculate SSres for the model y = 2x + 1
Two models are proposed. Use SSres to decide which fits better

methods.name: Table of residuals
methods.summary: For each point find observed y minus predicted y, square each residual and add; for (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 6) with y = 2x + 1 the residuals are 0, 0, −1 and SSres = 1.

methods.name: Residuals in GDC lists
methods.summary: Create a list of predictions from the model, a list of (y − prediction)², and use the list sum; or read the residual list stored after a regression.

misconceptions: Adding the residuals without squaring (giving −1 instead of 1), so positive and negative residuals cancel
Calculating predicted y minus observed y and thinking the sign matters for SSres
Comparing SSres between data sets with different units or sizes as if it were a fixed scale

skills.name: Find and interpret R², including its link to r for linear models
examTypes: Find the value of R² for the cubic model
Interpret the value R² = 0.92 in context
For a linear model R² = 0.81 and the gradient is negative. Find r

methods.name: Read R² from the regression output
methods.summary: Turn diagnostics on and read R² (or r² for linear) from the regression screen.

methods.name: R² = r² for a linear model
methods.summary: For a straight-line model, R² is the square of Pearson's r, so r = ±√R² with the sign of the gradient.

misconceptions: Taking r = +0.9 from R² = 0.81 when the gradient is negative (r = −0.9)
Interpreting R² = 0.92 as '92% of the points lie on the curve' instead of '92% of the variation in y is explained by the model'
Treating R² as a percentage chance that the model is correct

skills.name: Evaluate and compare regression models beyond R²
examTypes: The cubic model has a higher R² than the quadratic. Explain why it may still not be the better model
Comment on the validity of using the model to predict y when x = 50
Compare the two models and recommend one, giving two reasons

methods.name: Compare R² and SSres
methods.summary: Compare R² (and SSres) for the models, remembering that a cubic always fits at least as well as a quadratic or linear model on the same data, so a small gain may not matter.

methods.name: Check sense in context and range
methods.summary: Check whether the model gives realistic values in context, whether a prediction is interpolation or extrapolation, and whether the simpler model is good enough.

methods.name: Plot the curves over the data
methods.summary: Graph each model with the scatter to see patterns in the residuals and how the curves behave beyond the data.

misconceptions: Always picking the model with the highest R², even if it predicts negative populations
Thinking a high R² makes extrapolation far beyond the data reliable
Comparing R² for an exponential model with R² for a linear model as if they measured fit the same way (the GDC exponential R² refers to ln y)

subtopics.title: Linear combinations of random variables and unbiased estimates
subtopics.guide: Expectation and variance of a linear transformation aX + b; the expected value of any linear combination of random variables and the variance of a linear combination of independent random variables; x̄ as an unbiased estimate of μ and s²ₙ₋₁ = n/(n − 1) × s²ₙ as an unbiased estimate of σ². Proofs that these estimators are unbiased are not examined.

skills.name: Find E(aX + b) and Var(aX + b)
examTypes: E(X) = 4 and Var(X) = 5. Find E(3X + 2) and Var(3X + 2)
Each score is doubled and 10 is added. Find the new mean and standard deviation
A temperature in °C has mean 20 and variance 4. Find the mean and variance in °F

methods.name: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b, Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X)
methods.summary: Scale and shift the mean; scale the variance by a² and ignore b, because adding a constant moves the distribution without spreading it.

methods.name: Transform the distribution table
methods.summary: For a small discrete distribution, transform each value, then recompute the mean and variance on the GDC to check the rules.

misconceptions: Var(3X + 2) = 3 × 5 = 15, forgetting to square the 3
Multiplying the standard deviation by a² instead of |a|
Var(−2X) = −4Var(X), giving a negative variance

threads.echo: Adding b translates the distribution, so the mean moves but the variance does not; multiplying by a stretches it, so the spread scales: the same rule as translating and stretching a graph.

skills.name: Find the expected value of a linear combination of random variables
examTypes: Find the expected total cost of a meal of a starter, a main and a dessert
E(X) = 12 and E(Y) = 7. Find E(2X − 3Y + 5)
Find the expected profit, given the expected numbers of each item sold

methods.name: Linearity of expectation
methods.summary: E(a₁X₁ + a₂X₂ + … + b) = a₁E(X₁) + a₂E(X₂) + … + b, which holds whether or not the variables are independent.

methods.name: Add the averages in context
methods.summary: Write the total as a sum of the separate parts, then add the expected value of each part with its coefficient.

misconceptions: Thinking expectation only adds for independent variables
E(2X − 3Y + 5) = 24 − 21 = 3, forgetting the + 5 (correct is 8)
Squaring the coefficients when finding an expectation, as for variance

skills.name: Find the variance of a linear combination of independent random variables
examTypes: X and Y are independent with variances 9 and 16. Find Var(X − Y)
Find the standard deviation of the total mass of three different independent items
Explain why Var(X₁ + X₂) is not equal to Var(2X)

methods.name: Var(aX ± bY) = a²Var(X) + b²Var(Y)
methods.summary: For independent variables, square each coefficient, multiply by that variable's variance and add, even when the combination has a minus sign.

methods.name: Work in variances, then take the root
methods.summary: Convert every standard deviation to a variance, combine the variances, and only take the square root at the end.

misconceptions: Var(X − Y) = 9 − 16 = −7 instead of 9 + 16 = 25
Adding standard deviations: SD(X − Y) = 3 + 4 = 7 instead of √25 = 5
Treating X₁ + X₂ as 2X, giving variance 4σ² instead of 2σ²

skills.name: Find an unbiased estimate of the population mean
examTypes: Find an unbiased estimate of the population mean from the sample
Use the frequency table to find an unbiased estimate of μ
Find Σx given n = 20 and an unbiased estimate of μ of 14.5

methods.name: One-variable statistics
methods.summary: Enter the data (with frequencies if given) and read x̄, which is an unbiased estimate of μ.

methods.name: x̄ = Σx / n
methods.summary: Add all the values (Σfx for a frequency table) and divide by the total frequency; rearrange to Σx = n × x̄ when the sum is unknown.

misconceptions: Dividing Σfx by the number of rows in the table instead of Σf
Dividing by n − 1 when estimating the mean, as for the variance

skills.name: Find an unbiased estimate of the population variance
examTypes: Find an unbiased estimate of the population variance
A sample of 10 has variance s²ₙ = 4.5. Find s²ₙ₋₁
Explain why the GDC value σx should not be used as the estimate

methods.name: Square Sx from the GDC
methods.summary: Run one-variable statistics and square sx (the sample standard deviation with divisor n − 1) to get s²ₙ₋₁.

methods.name: s²ₙ₋₁ = n/(n − 1) × s²ₙ
methods.summary: Multiply the divisor-n variance by n/(n − 1), so n = 10 and s²ₙ = 4.5 give 10/9 × 4.5 = 5.

misconceptions: Squaring σx (divisor n) instead of sx, giving 4.5 instead of 5
Reporting sx (a standard deviation) when the variance was asked for
Multiplying by (n − 1)/n instead of n/(n − 1), giving 4.05 instead of 5

subtopics.title: Combining normal variables and the central limit theorem
subtopics.guide: Any linear combination of independent normal variables is normal, so X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) when X ~ N(μ, σ²); the central limit theorem says the sample mean is approximately normal for large samples from any distribution, with n > 30 taken as large enough in exams.

skills.name: Find probabilities for sums and differences of independent normal variables
examTypes: X ~ N(50, 3²) and Y ~ N(40, 4²) are independent. Find P(X − Y > 12)
Find the probability that a randomly chosen man is taller than a randomly chosen woman
Find the probability that the total mass of a box and its contents exceeds 2 kg

methods.name: Build the combined normal distribution
methods.summary: Find the mean and variance of the combination with the linear combination rules, for example X − Y ~ N(10, 25), then use normalcdf on that distribution.

methods.name: Turn a comparison into a difference
methods.summary: Rewrite P(X > Y) as P(X − Y > 0) so a comparison of two variables becomes a single normal probability.

misconceptions: Using variance 9 − 16 or standard deviation 4 − 3 = 1 for X − Y instead of standard deviation 5
Entering the variance 25 into normalcdf where the standard deviation 5 is needed
Finding P(X > 50) and P(Y < 40) separately and multiplying them to get P(X > Y)

threads.echo: The probability is still the area under the new normal curve, found by the same normalcdf integral as for a single variable.

skills.name: Distinguish the sum of n independent copies from n times one variable
examTypes: Find the probability that the total mass of 4 randomly chosen apples exceeds 850 g
Four apples are chosen at random. Explain why 4X and X₁ + X₂ + X₃ + X₄ have different distributions
Find the probability that 3 bags weigh more than 2 boxes in total

methods.name: Sum of n copies: N(nμ, nσ²)
methods.summary: For n independent observations, the total has mean nμ and variance nσ²; for one observation multiplied by n, the variance is n²σ². With X ~ N(200, 10²), the total of 4 has SD 20 but 4X has SD 40.

methods.name: Write out every variable
methods.summary: Write the total as X₁ + X₂ + … with each independent item named, then apply the variance rule term by term.

misconceptions: Using 4X ~ N(800, 1600) for the total of 4 independent apples instead of N(800, 400)
Using standard deviation 4 × 10 = 40 for the total of 4 independent items instead of 20
Using variance nσ² when the question really is about one item scaled by n

skills.name: Use X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) to find probabilities about a sample mean
examTypes: A sample of 25 is taken from N(80, 10²). Find P(X̄ > 83)
Write down the distribution of the sample mean
Find the least sample size so that P(|X̄ − μ| < 1) > 0.95

methods.name: normalcdf with σ/√n
methods.summary: Use normalcdf with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n, so for n = 25 and σ = 10 the standard deviation of X̄ is 2.

methods.name: Table of values for n
methods.summary: To find the least n, write the probability as a function of n and use a GDC table to find where it first passes the target.

methods.name: Solve with the inverse normal
methods.summary: Set the margin equal to z × σ/√n with z from invNorm, solve for n and round up to the next integer.

misconceptions: Using σ/n = 0.4 instead of σ/√n = 2 as the standard deviation of X̄
Using σ²/n = 4 as the standard deviation instead of the variance
Rounding the least sample size down instead of up

skills.name: Apply the central limit theorem to a sample mean from a non-normal population
examTypes: The waiting times are not normally distributed. Explain why the mean of 40 waiting times can be modelled as normal
Estimate the probability that the mean of 50 rolls of a die exceeds 3.8
Explain why the central limit theorem cannot be used for a sample of size 8

methods.name: Approximate X̄ by N(μ, σ²/n)
methods.summary: For n > 30, use the population mean and variance (for a fair die μ = 3.5, σ² = 35/12) to model X̄ as approximately N(μ, σ²/n) and find the probability on the GDC.

methods.name: Check which result applies
methods.summary: If the population is normal, X̄ is exactly normal for any n; if not, it is only approximately normal and needs a large sample, n > 30 in exams.

misconceptions: Thinking the central limit theorem makes the individual data values normal, rather than the sample mean
Thinking a sample from a normal population needs n > 30 before X̄ is normal
Using σ² instead of σ²/n for the variance of the sample mean

subtopics.title: Confidence intervals for a mean
subtopics.guide: Confidence intervals for the mean of a normal population, using the normal distribution when σ is known and the t-distribution when σ is unknown, whatever the sample size, and interpreting the interval in context.

skills.name: Find a confidence interval for μ when σ is known
examTypes: The population standard deviation is 6. Find a 95% confidence interval for the mean
Find a 90% confidence interval for μ from the sample data
Write down the value of z used for a 99% interval

methods.name: ZInterval on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter σ, the data or x̄ and n, and the confidence level, and read the lower and upper limits.

methods.name: x̄ ± z × σ/√n
methods.summary: Find z with invNorm (1.96 for 95%), multiply by σ/√n and add and subtract; with x̄ = 50, σ = 6, n = 36 this gives (48.04, 51.96).

misconceptions: Using σ instead of σ/√n, giving 50 ± 11.76 instead of 50 ± 1.96
Using z = 1.645 for a 95% interval (that is the value for 90%)
Using a t-interval when σ is given in the question

threads.echo: The interval sits symmetrically about x̄ because the normal curve is symmetric, so the same z is added and subtracted.

skills.name: Find a confidence interval for μ when σ is unknown
examTypes: Find a 95% confidence interval for the mean mass from the sample
Explain why the t-distribution is used here
Write down the number of degrees of freedom of the t-distribution

methods.name: TInterval on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter the data (or x̄, sₙ₋₁ and n) and the confidence level, and read the interval; the GDC uses n − 1 degrees of freedom.

methods.name: x̄ ± t × sₙ₋₁/√n
methods.summary: Use the t value with n − 1 degrees of freedom and the unbiased standard deviation sₙ₋₁; the interval is wider than the z-interval would be.

misconceptions: Using the normal distribution because n is large, when σ is unknown (the guide says use t regardless of n)
Entering σx (divisor n) instead of sx (divisor n − 1) into TInterval, making the interval too narrow
Using n degrees of freedom instead of n − 1

skills.name: Interpret a confidence interval in context and use it to judge a claim
examTypes: Interpret the 95% confidence interval in context
The manufacturer claims the mean is 500 ml. Does the interval support this claim?
The confidence intervals for two brands overlap. Comment on whether one brand is better

methods.name: Repeated-sampling meaning
methods.summary: If many samples were taken and an interval built from each, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true mean μ.

methods.name: Is the claimed value inside?
methods.summary: A claimed mean inside the interval is plausible; one outside it gives evidence against the claim at the matching significance level.

misconceptions: Saying there is a 95% probability that μ lies in this particular interval
Saying 95% of the data values lie in the interval
Concluding that brand A has a higher mean because its interval's midpoint is higher, even though the intervals overlap a lot

skills.name: Work backwards from an interval and reason about its width
examTypes: A 95% confidence interval is (12.3, 15.7). Find the sample mean
Find the least sample size so that the 95% interval has width less than 2
Explain the effect on the interval of increasing the confidence level

methods.name: Midpoint and half-width
methods.summary: The sample mean is the midpoint of the interval and the margin is half the width: (12.3, 15.7) gives x̄ = 14.0 and margin 1.7, which can then be set equal to z × σ/√n to find σ or n.

methods.name: Table of widths
methods.summary: Write the width 2z × σ/√n as a function of n and use a GDC table to find the first n that meets the requirement.

misconceptions: Taking the full width 3.4 as the margin instead of half of it
Thinking a higher confidence level gives a narrower interval
Thinking doubling n halves the width (it divides the width by √2)

subtopics.title: The Poisson distribution
subtopics.guide: The Poisson distribution as a model for independent events occurring at a uniform average rate, with mean and variance both equal to λ; the sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson; choosing between normal, binomial and Poisson models in context. Proofs of mean and variance are not required.

skills.name: Calculate Poisson probabilities with technology
examTypes: Calls arrive at a mean rate of 3 per hour. Find the probability of exactly 2 calls in an hour
Find the probability of at least 2 typing errors on a page
Find the probability that more than 5 cars pass in a minute

methods.name: poissonpdf and poissoncdf
methods.summary: Use poissonpdf(λ, k) for P(X = k) and poissoncdf(λ, k) for P(X ≤ k); for P(X ≥ k) use 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1).

methods.name: P(X = k) = e^(−λ) λᵏ / k!
methods.summary: Substitute directly, for example λ = 3, k = 2 gives e^(−3) × 9/2 ≈ 0.224; add terms for small cumulative probabilities.

misconceptions: Calculating P(X ≥ 2) as 1 − P(X ≤ 2) instead of 1 − P(X ≤ 1) (0.577 instead of 0.801 for λ = 3)
Using poissoncdf when the question asks for exactly k events
Treating 'more than 5' as P(X ≥ 5)

skills.name: Adjust the Poisson mean to a different interval
examTypes: Calls arrive at 3 per hour. Find the probability of at least 2 calls in 30 minutes
Find the probability of no faults in a 250 m length of cable, given 0.8 faults per 100 m
Find the length of time for which the probability of no arrivals is 0.1

methods.name: Scale λ in proportion
methods.summary: Because the rate is uniform, the mean is proportional to the interval length: 3 per hour becomes λ = 1.5 per 30 minutes, and P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − poissoncdf(1.5, 1) ≈ 0.442.

methods.name: Solve for an unknown interval
methods.summary: Write λ = rate × t, set the probability expression equal to the target and solve, for example e^(−3t) = 0.1 gives t = ln 10 / 3 ≈ 0.768 hours.

misconceptions: Using λ = 3 for a 30-minute interval because the rate was given per hour
Doubling λ instead of halving it when the interval is halved
Multiplying probabilities for one hour by 0.5 instead of changing λ

threads.echo: λ per unit time is a constant rate, so the mean for any interval is rate × length, just as distance is speed × time.

skills.name: Use mean = variance = λ to find λ or to judge whether a Poisson model fits
examTypes: The sample mean is 2.4 and the sample variance is 5.1. Comment on whether a Poisson model is suitable
Given P(X = 0) = 0.1, find λ
Write down the variance of the number of goals per match

methods.name: Compare sample mean and variance
methods.summary: Find x̄ and s² on the GDC; values that are close support a Poisson model, while a variance much larger or smaller than the mean argues against it.

methods.name: Solve an equation in λ
methods.summary: From a given probability, write an equation such as e^(−λ) = 0.1 and solve to get λ = ln 10 ≈ 2.30, or use the GDC solver for equations like P(X ≤ 1) = 0.2.

methods.name: Graph the probability against λ
methods.summary: Plot y = P(X = k) as a function of λ and intersect with the target value.

misconceptions: Taking the standard deviation as λ instead of √λ
Accepting a Poisson model when the variance is twice the mean
Solving e^(−λ) = 0.1 as λ = ln 0.1 ≈ −2.30, a negative mean, instead of λ = −ln 0.1 = ln 10 ≈ 2.30

threads.echo: Finding λ from P(X = 0) = e^(−λ) means undoing the exponential with a logarithm.

skills.name: Use the sum of independent Poisson variables
examTypes: A shop receives emails at 2 per hour and calls at 3 per hour. Find the probability of more than 6 contacts in an hour
Find the probability of exactly 4 errors in total on two pages
Write down the distribution of X + Y

methods.name: Add the means
methods.summary: If X ~ Po(λ) and Y ~ Po(μ) are independent, X + Y ~ Po(λ + μ), so use a single Poisson calculation with mean λ + μ.

methods.name: List the cases
methods.summary: For a small total, add P(X = i)P(Y = j) over all pairs with i + j equal to the total; this checks the shortcut.

misconceptions: Multiplying the two probabilities P(X > 6) and P(Y > 6) instead of using Po(5)
Thinking X − Y is also Poisson
Adding the probabilities instead of the means

skills.name: Combine a Poisson probability with a binomial or other model in a multi-stage problem
examTypes: Find the probability that in 5 randomly chosen hours, exactly 3 have at least 2 calls
Given that at least one fault occurred, find the probability that exactly two occurred
Find the probability that the first hour with no arrivals is the fourth hour

methods.name: Poisson probability as the binomial p
methods.summary: Find p for one interval from the Poisson model, then use B(n, p) for how many intervals out of n have that property.

methods.name: Conditional probability with Poisson values
methods.summary: Use P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) with the needed Poisson probabilities, for example P(X = 2 | X ≥ 1) = P(X = 2)/(1 − P(X = 0)).

misconceptions: Using λ = 5 × 3 for the 5 hours when the question asks how many separate hours have a property
Forgetting the binomial coefficient and just using p³(1 − p)²
Using P(X = 2) as the answer to the conditional question without dividing by P(X ≥ 1)

threads.echo: Once each hour is a success or a failure, the count of successful hours follows the nCr pattern of the binomial distribution.

skills.name: Choose between normal, binomial and Poisson models and state the conditions
examTypes: State two assumptions needed for a Poisson model to be appropriate
Decide whether a binomial, Poisson or normal distribution is the best model. Justify
Explain why a Poisson model may not be suitable for the number of customers over a whole day

methods.name: Check the defining features
methods.summary: Binomial: a fixed number of independent trials with constant success probability. Poisson: a count of independent events in an interval with a uniform average rate and no upper limit. Normal: a continuous measurement, symmetric and bell-shaped.

methods.name: Check the data
methods.summary: If data are given, compare mean and variance (equal for Poisson, variance smaller than mean for binomial) and look at the shape of the distribution.

misconceptions: Choosing a binomial model for a count with no fixed number of trials
Ignoring that the rate changes through the day, which breaks the uniform-rate condition
Choosing a Poisson model for a continuous quantity such as waiting time

subtopics.title: Critical regions, tests for a mean, a proportion or a correlation, and type I and II errors
subtopics.guide: Critical values and critical regions; tests for a population mean using z when σ is known and t when σ is unknown, with matched pairs treated as one sample of differences; one-tailed tests for a proportion (binomial) and a mean (Poisson); testing ρ = 0 with technology; Type I and Type II errors and their probabilities for normal (known variance), binomial and Poisson tests. Critical regions for t-tests are not required, and for discrete tests the critical region is the largest one with probability below the significance level.

skills.name: Find the critical value and critical region for a test of a normal mean with σ known
examTypes: H₀: μ = 100, H₁: μ > 100, σ = 15, n = 25. Find the critical region for x̄ at the 5% level
Find the critical values for a two-tailed test at the 1% level
State whether a sample mean of 104 lies in the critical region

methods.name: invNorm on the distribution of X̄
methods.summary: Under H₀, X̄ ~ N(100, 3²); use invNorm(0.95, 100, 3) to get the critical value 104.93, so the critical region is x̄ > 104.93.

methods.name: μ₀ + z × σ/√n
methods.summary: Use z = 1.645 for a one-tailed 5% test (1.96 for each tail of a two-tailed 5% test) and convert: 100 + 1.645 × 15/5 ≈ 104.93.

methods.name: Shade the tail on a sketch
methods.summary: Sketch the normal curve of X̄ under H₀ and shade the tail area equal to the significance level on the side given by H₁.

misconceptions: Using σ instead of σ/√n, giving 100 + 1.645 × 15 = 124.7
Using 1.96 for a one-tailed 5% test, giving 105.88
Putting the whole 5% in one tail of a two-tailed test

threads.echo: The critical value comes from the inverse normal: it turns the tail area α back into a value of x̄.

skills.name: Test a population mean with a z-test or t-test, including matched pairs
examTypes: Test at the 5% level whether the mean weight is less than 500 g
The same students were timed before and after training. Test whether training reduced their times
Explain why a t-test is used rather than a z-test

methods.name: Z-Test or T-Test on the GDC
methods.summary: Use Z-Test when σ is known and T-Test when it is not, whatever the sample size; choose the alternative and compare the p-value with α.

methods.name: Reduce paired data to differences
methods.summary: For matched pairs, find d = after − before for each subject and run a one-sample t-test on the list of differences with H₀: μ_d = 0.

misconceptions: Running a two-sample unpaired test on before-and-after data from the same subjects
Using a z-test with s as σ because n is large, when σ is unknown
Calculating differences as before − after and then keeping H₁: μ_d < 0, which tests the opposite claim

skills.name: Carry out a one-tailed binomial test for a proportion and find its critical region
examTypes: H₀: p = 0.3, H₁: p > 0.3, n = 20. Find the critical region at the 5% level
In a sample of 20, 9 succeeded. Test at the 5% level whether the proportion has increased
Write down the actual significance level of the test

methods.name: p-value from the tail
methods.summary: Under H₀ find P(X ≥ observed) (or P(X ≤ observed) for H₁: p < p₀) with binomcdf and compare it with α; for 9 out of 20 with p = 0.3, P(X ≥ 9) = 0.113 > 0.05, so do not reject H₀.

methods.name: Table of tail probabilities
methods.summary: Tabulate P(X ≥ k) for several k and take the smallest k with probability below α: P(X ≥ 9) = 0.113, P(X ≥ 10) = 0.048, so the critical region is X ≥ 10.

misconceptions: Choosing X ≥ 9 because P(X ≥ 9) is the first value 'near' 5% (it is 0.113)
Choosing X ≥ 11, which keeps the probability below 5% but does not maximise it
Using P(X = 9) instead of P(X ≥ 9) as the p-value
Finding P(X ≥ 10) as 1 − P(X ≤ 10) instead of 1 − P(X ≤ 9)

threads.echo: The test statistic follows B(n, p₀), so the p-value is a sum of nCr pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ terms from the tail.

skills.name: Carry out a one-tailed Poisson test for a mean rate and find its critical region
examTypes: H₀: λ = 6, H₁: λ < 6. Find the critical region at the 5% level
After a safety campaign there were 2 accidents in a month. Test whether the rate has fallen
The mean was 2 per day. Over a week 21 were observed. Test whether the rate has increased

methods.name: p-value with poissoncdf
methods.summary: Under H₀ find the tail probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed and compare with α; scale λ first if the observation covers a different interval.

methods.name: Tabulate to find the critical region
methods.summary: For H₁: λ < 6, P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0174 and P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0620, so the largest region below 5% is X ≤ 1.

misconceptions: Taking the critical region as X ≤ 2 because 0.062 is close to 0.05
Testing a week's count against λ = 2 instead of λ = 14
Using P(X < 2) as the p-value for an observation of 2 under H₁: λ < 6, missing P(X = 2)

skills.name: Test whether the population correlation coefficient ρ is zero
examTypes: Test at the 5% level whether there is positive correlation between x and y in the population
State the hypotheses for a test of the correlation coefficient
Find the p-value and state the conclusion in context

methods.name: LinRegTTest on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter the paired data, choose the alternative ρ > 0, ρ < 0 or ρ ≠ 0, and read r and the p-value; compare p with α.

methods.name: Read the tail from the question
methods.summary: 'Positive correlation' gives H₁: ρ > 0, 'negative' gives ρ < 0, and 'any correlation' gives ρ ≠ 0, with H₀: ρ = 0 every time.

misconceptions: Writing the hypotheses in terms of r instead of the population coefficient ρ
Comparing r itself with the significance level (for example 'r = 0.04 < 0.05, so reject')
Concluding that x causes y after rejecting ρ = 0

skills.name: Define Type I and Type II errors and calculate their probabilities
examTypes: Describe a Type I error in context
Find the probability of a Type I error for the test
Given that in fact p = 0.5, find the probability of a Type II error

methods.name: Type I: P(in critical region | H₀)
methods.summary: For a normal test it equals α; for a discrete test it is the actual tail probability of the critical region, for example P(X ≥ 10 | p = 0.3) = 0.048.

methods.name: Type II: P(not in critical region | true value)
methods.summary: Use the stated true parameter: with critical region X ≥ 10 and true p = 0.5, P(X ≤ 9) ≈ 0.412; for the normal example, P(X̄ < 104.93 | μ = 106) ≈ 0.361.

methods.name: Decision-versus-truth table
methods.summary: Draw a 2 × 2 table of 'H₀ true / H₀ false' against 'reject / do not reject' to identify which cell each error is.

misconceptions: Mixing the two up: calling 'not rejecting a false H₀' a Type I error
Giving the Type I probability of a discrete test as 0.05 instead of the actual 0.048
Calculating the Type II probability using the H₀ value of the parameter instead of the true value
Thinking P(Type I) + P(Type II) = 1

subtopics.title: Transition matrices and Markov chains
subtopics.guide: Markov chains: transition diagrams and transition matrices T with Tᵢⱼ the probability of moving from state j to state i, initial state matrices, and the state after n steps sₙ = Tⁿs₀; regular Markov chains; steady-state and long-term probabilities found by high powers of T or by solving linear equations, seen as the eigenvector for eigenvalue 1.

skills.name: Build a transition matrix or transition diagram from a description
examTypes: Write down the transition matrix for the weather model
Draw a transition diagram for the information given
Find the missing entries in the transition matrix

methods.name: Columns are 'from', rows are 'to'
methods.summary: Put the probabilities of leaving state j in column j, so each column sums to 1; a sunny day followed by sun with probability 0.8 and rain 0.2 gives the first column (0.8, 0.2).

methods.name: Read arrows off the diagram
methods.summary: Each arrow from j to i labelled p becomes the entry in row i, column j; loops give the diagonal entries.

misconceptions: Writing the 'from' probabilities along rows, giving the transpose so the columns no longer sum to 1
Missing the probability of staying in the same state, so a column sums to less than 1
Finding a missing entry so that the row sums to 1 instead of the column

skills.name: Find the state matrix after n steps using sₙ = Tⁿs₀
examTypes: Today is sunny. Find the probability that it is sunny in 3 days' time
Initially 60% of customers use brand A. Find the expected proportion using brand A after 5 weeks
Find the probability that a person in state A is in state B after two transitions

methods.name: Matrix power on the GDC
methods.summary: Store T and s₀ as matrices and compute Tⁿs₀ directly; the entry for the required state is the probability or proportion.

methods.name: Multiply one step at a time
methods.summary: Compute s₁ = Ts₀, then s₂ = Ts₁, and so on; for small n this shows how the probabilities move.

methods.name: Tree diagram of paths
methods.summary: For two or three steps, add the probabilities of all paths that end in the required state; this matches the matrix entry.

misconceptions: Computing s₀Tⁿ (row times matrix) with this column convention, which is undefined or gives the wrong numbers
Calculating nT instead of Tⁿ
Using Tⁿ⁺¹ or Tⁿ⁻¹ by miscounting the number of transitions from day 0

threads.echo: Each step multiplies the state by the same matrix T, the matrix version of multiplying by the same ratio in a geometric sequence.

skills.name: Estimate the steady state from high powers of the transition matrix
examTypes: Find the long-term probability that a day is rainy
Calculate T²⁰ and explain what it tells you about the long-term behaviour
Show that the long-term proportions do not depend on the initial state

methods.name: Raise T to a large power
methods.summary: Compute T⁵⁰ (or similar) on the GDC; for a regular chain every column becomes the same steady-state vector, for example (0.6, 0.4).

methods.name: Iterate until the state stops changing
methods.summary: Keep multiplying the state by T until the entries agree to the required accuracy.

misconceptions: Stopping at a small power such as T⁵ where the columns still differ
Thinking the long-term state depends on the initial state for a regular chain
Reading a row of Tⁿ instead of a column as the steady-state vector

skills.name: Find the exact steady state by solving Ts = s
examTypes: Find the exact steady-state vector by solving a system of equations
Show that (0.6, 0.4) is the steady-state vector
Explain the connection between the steady state and an eigenvector of T

methods.name: Solve Ts = s with the entries summing to 1
methods.summary: Write the equations from Ts = s, replace one with a + b + … = 1 and solve; for T with columns (0.8, 0.2) and (0.3, 0.7), 0.2a = 0.3b and a + b = 1 give (0.6, 0.4).

methods.name: Eigenvector for eigenvalue 1
methods.summary: The steady state is the eigenvector of T with eigenvalue 1, scaled so its entries add to 1.

methods.name: Check by multiplying
methods.summary: Multiply T by the proposed vector; it is the steady state exactly when the result is the same vector.

misconceptions: Solving Ts = s without the condition that the entries sum to 1, and giving (0, 0) or an unscaled eigenvector such as (3, 2)
Using all the equations from Ts = s, which are dependent, and finding no unique solution
Solving sT = s with the column convention, which gives the wrong vector

threads.echo: Ts = s, (T − I)s = 0 and 'eigenvector for eigenvalue 1' are three forms of the same condition.

skills.name: Identify a regular Markov chain and interpret long-term results in context
examTypes: Explain why the Markov chain is regular
Interpret the steady-state vector in context
In the long run, how many of 2000 customers are expected to use brand B?

methods.name: Find a power with all positive entries
methods.summary: A chain is regular if some power of T has every entry strictly positive; compute T², T³, … on the GDC to find one.

methods.name: Check reachability on the diagram
methods.summary: Check that every state can be reached from every state and that the chain is not stuck in a fixed cycle; an absorbing state (probability 1 of staying) makes the chain not regular.

methods.name: Scale the steady state
methods.summary: Multiply the steady-state proportion by the population size and describe it as the long-run proportion, not a guaranteed count.

misconceptions: Thinking a chain is not regular because T itself has a zero entry, even though T² has none
Thinking a chain with an absorbing state is regular
Interpreting a steady-state entry of 0.4 as 'it will rain on exactly 4 of the next 10 days'

subtopics.title: Stationary points: local maxima and minima
subtopics.guide: Finding where a curve has zero gradient by solving f′(x) = 0, with technology used to produce f′ and to solve, and identifying local maximum and minimum points. Students should know that a local maximum or minimum need not be the greatest or least value of the function on a given domain; the second derivative test is not part of SL (it is AHL5.10).

skills.name: Find where the gradient is zero by solving f′(x) = 0
examTypes: Find f′(x) and hence the values of x where the gradient of the curve is zero
Use your GDC to solve f′(x) = 0
Find the x-coordinates of the points where the tangent is horizontal

methods.name: Differentiate, then solve
methods.summary: Use the power rule to find f′(x), set it equal to 0 and solve by factorising or the quadratic formula.

methods.name: GDC polynomial solver
methods.summary: Enter the coefficients of f′(x) in the polynomial or equation solver and read off the roots.

methods.name: Zeros of the f′ graph
methods.summary: Graph f′ (typed in, or generated by the GDC's derivative function) and find where it crosses the x-axis.

misconceptions: Solving f(x) = 0 instead of f′(x) = 0: for f(x) = x² − 4x this gives x = 0 and x = 4 instead of x = 2
Keeping the constant when differentiating: f(x) = x³ − 3x + 5 becomes f′(x) = 3x² + 2, which has no zeros, instead of 3x² − 3 with zeros x = ±1
Losing the negative root: 3x² − 12 = 0 gives only x = 2, missing x = −2

threads.echo: A horizontal tangent is the calculus signal for a possible maximum or minimum, the same point a parabola's vertex formula finds.
The zeros of f′ can be found by factorising, by the GDC solver, or as x-intercepts of the f′ graph, and each checks the others.

skills.name: Find the coordinates of a local maximum or minimum point
examTypes: Find the coordinates of the local maximum point of the curve
Write down the coordinates of the local minimum
Find the minimum value of the function and the value of x where it occurs

methods.name: Solve f′ = 0, then substitute into f
methods.summary: Find the x-coordinate from f′(x) = 0, then substitute it into f (not f′) for the y-coordinate.

methods.name: GDC maximum/minimum tool
methods.summary: Graph f on a window that shows the turning point and use the maximum or minimum feature.

methods.name: Vertex of a quadratic
methods.summary: For a quadratic the only stationary point is the vertex at x = −b/(2a).

misconceptions: Substituting into f′ instead of f: for f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 this gives (1, 0) instead of the local maximum (1, 5)
Giving only the x-coordinate when the coordinates or the minimum value are asked for
Reading a point where the graph leaves the GDC window as a turning point

threads.echo: The local maximum and minimum points are the turning points of the curve, found wherever the gradient is zero.

skills.name: Decide whether a stationary point is a local maximum or minimum
examTypes: Determine whether this stationary point is a maximum or a minimum. Justify your answer
Use the gradient either side of x = 3 to classify the point
State the nature of each stationary point

methods.name: Sign of f′ either side
methods.summary: Evaluate f′ just to the left and right: + then − is a maximum, − then + is a minimum.

methods.name: Shape of the GDC graph
methods.summary: Graph f and see whether the curve peaks or dips at the point; good evidence, but say what you looked at.

methods.name: Shape of a cubic
methods.summary: For a cubic with a positive x³ coefficient and two stationary points, the left one is the maximum and the right one the minimum.

misconceptions: Reversing the rule: calling + then − a minimum
Checking the sign of f, not f′, either side of the point
Testing points beyond the next stationary point: for f′(x) = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), testing x = 0 and x = 4 around x = 1 gives + and +, so the maximum at x = 1 is missed

threads.echo: A maximum is where the rate of change switches from positive to negative: the output stops rising and starts falling.

skills.name: Find the greatest or least value of a function on a given domain
examTypes: Find the greatest value of f for 0 ≤ x ≤ 5
Explain why the local maximum is not the greatest value of f on this domain
Find the range of f on the given domain

methods.name: Compare stationary values with endpoints
methods.summary: Evaluate f at each stationary point inside the domain and at both endpoints; the largest and smallest of these are the greatest and least values.

methods.name: Graph on the domain
methods.summary: Set the GDC window to the domain and read the highest and lowest points, including the ends of the graph.

misconceptions: Giving the local maximum as the greatest value: for f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 5, answering 5 when f(5) = 21
Including a stationary point that lies outside the given domain
Forgetting to evaluate f at the endpoints at all

threads.echo: The biggest value on a closed interval can sit at an end of the interval, where the gradient is not zero.

skills.name: Locate and classify stationary points of f from the graph of f′
examTypes: The graph of f′ is shown. Write down the x-coordinate of the local maximum of f
Using the graph of f′, state the intervals where f is increasing
Which sketch could be the graph of f?

methods.name: Read signs from the f′ graph
methods.summary: Stationary points of f are where the f′ graph meets the x-axis; f′ crossing from above to below is a maximum, from below to above a minimum.

methods.name: Build a sign diagram
methods.summary: Mark the zeros of f′ on a number line with the sign of f′ in each interval, then sketch f rising and falling to match.

misconceptions: Taking the turning points of the f′ graph as the stationary points of f
Reading f′ crossing from negative to positive as a maximum
Calling a point where f′ touches the axis without changing sign a maximum or minimum (it is neither)

threads.echo: The f′ graph is a graph of rates: above the axis f rises, below it f falls, and on the axis f is momentarily level.

subtopics.title: Optimisation in context
subtopics.guide: Solving optimisation problems in context with calculus and technology: maximising profit or volume, minimising cost or material, including setting up the function from a constraint such as a fixed volume or surface area. Kinematics optimisation is not set at SL.

skills.name: Find the optimum of a given model in context
examTypes: The profit from selling x items is P(x). Find the number of items that maximises the profit
Find the minimum cost and the value of x where it occurs
Show that this value of x gives a maximum

methods.name: Set the derivative to zero
methods.summary: Differentiate the model, solve the derivative = 0, check it is a maximum or minimum, then answer the question asked.

methods.name: GDC maximum/minimum
methods.summary: Graph the model on a window that fits the context and use the maximum or minimum tool.

methods.name: Vertex of a quadratic model
methods.summary: If the model is quadratic, the optimum is at x = −b/(2a).

misconceptions: Giving the x-value when the optimum value is asked: for P(x) = −0.5x² + 40x − 300, answering 40 when the maximum profit is 500
Optimising revenue instead of profit (profit = revenue − cost)
Reporting a minimum when a maximum was wanted because the derivative = 0 was not checked

threads.echo: An optimum in context is a turning point of the model, found where its rate of change is zero.

skills.name: Set up the function to optimise using a constraint
examTypes: A closed cylinder has volume 500 cm³. Show that its surface area is A = 2πr² + 1000/r
An open box is made by cutting squares of side x from a 20 cm square sheet. Show that V = x(20 − 2x)²
Write the profit as a function of x, given the revenue and cost functions

methods.name: Rearrange the constraint and substitute
methods.summary: Use the fixed quantity to express one variable in terms of the other (h = 500/(πr²)), then substitute into the quantity to optimise.

methods.name: Label the net or diagram
methods.summary: Draw the shape with every dimension written in terms of x before writing the formula.

misconceptions: Forgetting that both sides of the box lose a square: V = x(20 − x)² instead of x(20 − 2x)²
Using πrh for the curved surface, giving A = 2πr² + 500/r instead of 2πr² + 1000/r
Including a lid on an open container: 2πr² + 2V/r instead of πr² + 2V/r

threads.echo: Rewriting the surface area in one variable does not change it; it changes it into a form the derivative can be used on.

skills.name: Solve a full packaging or design optimisation
examTypes: Find the radius that minimises the surface area of a can of fixed volume
Find the value of x that maximises the volume of the box, and the maximum volume
Find the dimensions that use the least material

methods.name: Differentiate the one-variable model
methods.summary: Set up A(r) or V(x), solve A′(r) = 0 (for A = 2πr² + 1000/r this gives r³ = 250/π, r ≈ 4.30 cm), and justify the minimum.

methods.name: Graph the model
methods.summary: Graph A(r) or V(x) on the GDC over the sensible domain and use the minimum or maximum tool.

misconceptions: Accepting the root x = 10 for the 20 cm box, which gives zero volume, instead of x = 10/3 with V ≈ 593 cm³
Rounding r to 4.3 before finding h, so the height and area come out slightly wrong
Stopping at the value of r when the question asks for the minimum area

threads.echo: The best container is a turning point of its area or volume function, found by the same f′ = 0 idea as any maximum or minimum.

skills.name: Interpret and adjust an optimum to fit the context
examTypes: The number of items must be a whole number. Find the maximum profit
State the domain of V in this context
Explain why the answer from the derivative cannot be used directly

methods.name: Test neighbouring whole numbers
methods.summary: If the optimum x is not a whole number, evaluate the model at the integers either side and keep the better one.

methods.name: GDC table of values
methods.summary: Tabulate the model for whole-number inputs near the optimum and read off the best.

methods.name: Check the domain
methods.summary: Find the realistic domain (lengths positive, box sides 20 − 2x > 0) and compare with the endpoint values.

misconceptions: Rounding the optimum x to the nearest whole number without checking the neighbouring integer, which can give the smaller value
Giving a negative length or a box side of 20 − 2x < 0 as a valid answer
Leaving out units, or giving cm² for a volume

threads.echo: A real-world optimum must respect the domain: the calculus answer is a candidate, the context picks the final one.

subtopics.title: Approximating areas with the trapezoidal rule
subtopics.guide: Estimating an area with the trapezoidal rule using intervals of equal width, from a function or from a table of data such as measurements of an irregular shape. Includes comparing the estimate with the true value and saying whether it is an over- or underestimate.

skills.name: Estimate an integral of a given function with the trapezoidal rule
examTypes: Use the trapezoidal rule with 4 intervals to estimate the area under the curve from x = 0 to x = 2
Write down the value of h and use it to estimate the integral
Complete the table of values and hence estimate the area

methods.name: Trapezoidal rule formula
methods.summary: With h = (b − a)/n, area ≈ (h/2)[y₀ + yₙ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁)]; for y = x² on [0, 2] with n = 4 this gives 2.75.

methods.name: Add the trapezia one by one
methods.summary: Find each strip's area ½h(yᵢ + yᵢ₊₁) and add them; this gives the same total as the formula.

methods.name: GDC list or spreadsheet
methods.summary: Put the y-values in a list, apply the weights 1, 2, …, 2, 1, sum and multiply by h/2.

misconceptions: Using h = 2/5 because there are 5 y-values, instead of h = 2/4 = 0.5
Not doubling the inner heights: 0.25(0 + 0.25 + 1 + 2.25 + 4) = 1.875 instead of 2.75
Leaving out the ½: 0.5(0 + 4 + 2 × 3.5) = 5.5 instead of 2.75

threads.echo: The trapezoidal rule adds up the areas of thin strips, the same idea the definite integral makes exact.

skills.name: Estimate an area or total from a table of measurements
examTypes: The widths of a lake are measured every 10 m. Estimate the area of the lake
A car's speed is recorded every 5 seconds. Estimate the distance travelled
Use the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of the field

methods.name: Formula with tabulated heights
methods.summary: Read h from the equal spacing of the measurements and the yᵢ from the table, then apply (h/2)[ends + 2 × middles].

methods.name: Strip by strip
methods.summary: Draw the shape cut into strips of equal width, find each trapezium area and add.

misconceptions: Using the spacing values as the heights and the measurements as the widths
Mixing units: speeds in m/s with times recorded in minutes, so the distance is 60 times too small
Treating the first and last widths as interior values and doubling them

threads.echo: Distance from a speed table is speed × time added over small intervals, the same 'area under a graph' as an integral.

skills.name: Compare a trapezoidal estimate with the exact value
examTypes: Use your GDC to find the exact value of the integral
Find the percentage error in the trapezoidal estimate
Explain how the estimate could be improved

methods.name: GDC definite integral
methods.summary: Find the exact value with the GDC's integral function and compare.

methods.name: Percentage error
methods.summary: Percentage error = |estimate − exact| / exact × 100%; for 2.75 against 8/3 this is 3.125%.

misconceptions: Dividing by the estimate instead of the exact value: 0.0833/2.75 ≈ 3.03% instead of 3.13%
Thinking that using more strips makes the estimate less accurate
Giving a negative percentage error instead of using the absolute difference

threads.echo: As the strips get thinner the sum of trapezia approaches the definite integral.

skills.name: Decide whether the trapezoidal rule over- or underestimates
examTypes: State, with a reason, whether the estimate is greater or less than the true area
Use the graph to explain why the trapezoidal rule overestimates here
Which of these curves gives an underestimate?

methods.name: Draw the chords
methods.summary: Join the tops of the strips with straight lines: if the chords lie above the curve (curve bends upwards) it is an overestimate, below it (curve bends downwards) an underestimate.

methods.name: Compare with the GDC value
methods.summary: Calculate the integral on the GDC and see which side of it the estimate falls.

misconceptions: Deciding from whether the curve rises: y = √x is increasing, but the trapezoidal rule underestimates it
Assuming the trapezoidal rule always overestimates
Thinking a straight-line graph gives an error (the rule is exact for a line)

threads.echo: The shape of the graph answers 'over or under' before any calculation; the GDC integral confirms it.

skills.name: Find an unknown height from a given trapezoidal estimate
examTypes: The trapezoidal estimate of the area is 12.5. Find the value of k in the table
Find the missing width given the estimated area of the lake

methods.name: Set up a linear equation
methods.summary: Write the trapezoidal sum with k in its place (weight 1 at an end, 2 in the middle), set it equal to the estimate and solve.

methods.name: GDC solver
methods.summary: Enter the trapezoidal expression with k into the equation solver.

misconceptions: Giving an interior unknown weight 1 instead of 2, so k comes out roughly double
Forgetting the h/2 factor when setting up the equation

threads.echo: Working back from the estimate to the missing height undoes the trapezoidal calculation step by step.

subtopics.title: Further differentiation: standard derivatives, chain, product and quotient rules, related rates
subtopics.guide: Differentiating sin x, cos x, tan x, eˣ, ln x and xⁿ for rational n, and combining them with the chain, product and quotient rules. Applying derivatives to related rates of change and, through the link to SL5.6 and SL5.7, to stationary points and optimisation.

skills.name: Differentiate the standard functions
examTypes: Find f′(x) for f(x) = 3 sin x − 2eˣ + ln x
Differentiate y = 4√x − 2/x²
Find the gradient of y = tan x at x = π/4

methods.name: Use the standard results
methods.summary: sin x → cos x, cos x → −sin x, tan x → 1/cos²x, eˣ → eˣ, ln x → 1/x, xⁿ → nxⁿ⁻¹.

methods.name: Rewrite roots and fractions as powers
methods.summary: Write √x = x^(1/2) and 2/x² = 2x⁻² before using the power rule.

methods.name: Check a gradient on the GDC
methods.summary: Compare your f′(a) with the GDC's numerical derivative at x = a.

misconceptions: d/dx(cos x) = sin x, losing the minus sign
Applying the power rule to eˣ: d/dx(eˣ) = x·eˣ⁻¹
d/dx(x⁻²) = −2x⁻¹ (power raised instead of lowered) instead of −2x⁻³

threads.echo: Every standard derivative is a formula for the gradient of the curve at any point.

skills.name: Differentiate a composite function with the chain rule
examTypes: Differentiate y = sin(3x²)
Find the derivative of e^(−0.5x)
Find f′(x) for f(x) = ln(2x + 1)

methods.name: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx
methods.summary: Let u be the inside function, differentiate outer and inner separately and multiply.

methods.name: Outer derivative times inner derivative
methods.summary: Differentiate the outer function leaving the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside: d/dx ln(2x + 1) = 2/(2x + 1).

methods.name: GDC numerical check
methods.summary: Check the gradient at one x-value against the GDC's numerical derivative.

misconceptions: Forgetting the inner derivative: d/dx sin(3x²) = cos(3x²) instead of 6x cos(3x²)
d/dx ln(2x + 1) = 1/(2x + 1) instead of 2/(2x + 1)
Differentiating inside the bracket: d/dx sin(3x²) = cos(6x)

threads.echo: Rates multiply along a chain: if y changes 3 times as fast as u and u twice as fast as x, y changes 6 times as fast as x.

skills.name: Differentiate a product with the product rule
examTypes: Differentiate y = x²eˣ
Find f′(x) for f(x) = x sin x
Show that the derivative of x ln x is ln x + 1

methods.name: u′v + uv′
methods.summary: Differentiate each factor and combine: d/dx(x²eˣ) = 2xeˣ + x²eˣ.

methods.name: Expand first when possible
methods.summary: If both factors are polynomials, multiply out and use the power rule instead.

methods.name: GDC numerical check
methods.summary: Compare the gradient at one point with the GDC's numerical derivative.

misconceptions: Multiplying the derivatives: d/dx(x²eˣ) = 2xeˣ
Using only one term of the rule: d/dx(x sin x) = x cos x
d/dx(x ln x) = ln x, forgetting the x × 1/x = 1 term

threads.echo: Expanding a polynomial product and using the product rule give the same derivative, so one checks the other.

skills.name: Differentiate a quotient with the quotient rule
examTypes: Differentiate y = sin x / x
Find f′(x) for f(x) = eˣ/(x + 1)
Use the quotient rule to show that d/dx(tan x) = 1/cos²x

methods.name: (vu′ − uv′)/v²
methods.summary: With u on top and v below, f′ = (vu′ − uv′)/v²: d/dx(sin x / x) = (x cos x − sin x)/x².

methods.name: Rewrite as a product
methods.summary: Write u/v as u·v⁻¹ and use the product and chain rules.

methods.name: GDC numerical check
methods.summary: Check the gradient at one x-value on the GDC.

misconceptions: Reversing the numerator: (sin x − x cos x)/x²
Forgetting to square the denominator: (x cos x − sin x)/x
Dividing the derivatives: d/dx(sin x / x) = cos x / 1 = cos x

threads.echo: sin x/cos x and tan x are the same function, so the quotient rule must give the standard result 1/cos²x.

skills.name: Find a rate of change using related rates
examTypes: A spherical balloon is inflated at 50 cm³ s⁻¹. Find the rate of increase of the radius when r = 5 cm
The radius of a circular ripple grows at 2 cm s⁻¹. Find the rate of increase of the area when r = 10
Find dh/dt when the water depth is 3 m

methods.name: Link the rates with the chain rule
methods.summary: Write dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt; with V = (4/3)πr³, dV/dr = 4πr² = 100π at r = 5, so dr/dt = 50/(100π) ≈ 0.159 cm s⁻¹.

methods.name: Differentiate the relation with respect to t
methods.summary: Differentiate both sides of the formula with respect to t, then substitute the known values.

misconceptions: Substituting r = 5 before differentiating, so V is a constant and the rate comes out as 0
Multiplying instead of dividing: dr/dt = 50 × 100π
Using the surface area formula 4πr² as the volume

threads.echo: Related rates turn one known rate into another through the gradient that connects the two quantities.

skills.name: Use the further rules to find stationary points, tangents and normals
examTypes: Find the coordinates of the maximum point of y = xe⁻ˣ
Find the equation of the tangent to y = ln(2x + 1) at x = 0
Find the x-coordinate where the gradient of the curve is zero

methods.name: Differentiate and solve
methods.summary: Find f′ with the appropriate rule, factorise (xe⁻ˣ gives e⁻ˣ(1 − x)), and use eˣ > 0 to solve: maximum at (1, 1/e).

methods.name: GDC maximum and tangent tools
methods.summary: Graph the function and use the maximum or tangent feature, or the numerical derivative at a point.

misconceptions: Using half the product rule: d/dx(xe⁻ˣ) = −xe⁻ˣ, which suggests the only stationary point is x = 0
Writing e⁻ˣ = 0 as a solution of e⁻ˣ(1 − x) = 0
Using the gradient of the tangent in the normal's equation instead of its negative reciprocal

threads.echo: With more functions to differentiate, the same f′(x) = 0 test now finds the maxima of exponential and trigonometric models.

subtopics.title: The second derivative and the second derivative test
subtopics.guide: The second derivative in both notations, d²y/dx² and f″(x), and its use in the second derivative test for maxima and minima. Concave-up (f″ > 0) and concave-down (f″ < 0), and points of inflexion as points where the concavity changes, interpreted in context.

skills.name: Find the second derivative
examTypes: Find d²y/dx²
Find f″(x) and evaluate f″(2)
Find the second derivative of the displacement and interpret it

methods.name: Differentiate twice
methods.summary: Differentiate f to get f′, then differentiate f′ again: f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 gives f″(x) = 6x − 12.

methods.name: GDC numerical second derivative
methods.summary: Nest the GDC's derivative function to evaluate f″ at a point and check the algebra.

misconceptions: Squaring the first derivative: (dy/dx)² instead of d²y/dx²
Losing a sign: for y = sin 2x giving d²y/dx² = 4 sin 2x instead of −4 sin 2x
Differentiating f instead of f′ the second time, so f″ = f′

threads.echo: The second derivative is the rate of change of the gradient: how fast the slope itself is changing.

skills.name: Classify stationary points with the second derivative test
examTypes: Use the second derivative to show that this point is a local maximum
Determine the nature of each stationary point
Explain why the test gives no conclusion at x = 0 for y = x⁴

methods.name: Sign of f″ at the point
methods.summary: f″ > 0 gives a local minimum, f″ < 0 a local maximum; for x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1, f″(1) = −6 (maximum) and f″(3) = 6 (minimum).

methods.name: First derivative sign check
methods.summary: Check the sign of f′ either side; use this when f″ = 0 at the point.

methods.name: Look at the GDC graph
methods.summary: Graph f to support the classification.

misconceptions: Reversing the test: f″ > 0 means a maximum
Treating f″(a) = 0 as proof of a point of inflexion (y = x⁴ has a minimum at 0 with f″(0) = 0)
Substituting the y-coordinate into f″ instead of the x-coordinate

threads.echo: A curve that bends upwards (concave up) at a stationary point must be at a minimum, so the sign of f″ decides max or min.

skills.name: Find where a curve is concave up or concave down
examTypes: Find the interval on which the graph is concave down
Show that f is concave up for all x
State the values of x for which f″(x) > 0

methods.name: Solve f″(x) > 0 or < 0
methods.summary: Solve the inequality: f″(x) = 6x − 12 > 0 gives concave up for x > 2 and concave down for x < 2.

methods.name: Graph f″
methods.summary: Graph f″ on the GDC and read where it lies above or below the x-axis.

methods.name: Trend of the f′ graph
methods.summary: f is concave up where f′ is increasing and concave down where f′ is decreasing.

misconceptions: Using f′ > 0 (increasing) for concave up
Swapping the terms: calling f″ < 0 concave up
Giving the concavity at a single point instead of an interval

threads.echo: Concave up means the gradient is increasing, so the sign of f″ tells you whether the rate of change is growing or shrinking.

skills.name: Find a point of inflexion and check the concavity changes
examTypes: Find the coordinates of the point of inflexion
Show that the curve has a point of inflexion at x = 2
Explain why f″(0) = 0 does not mean there is a point of inflexion at x = 0

methods.name: f″ = 0 with a sign change
methods.summary: Solve f″(x) = 0, then check f″ changes sign either side; for x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 this is (2, 3).

methods.name: Turning point of the f′ graph
methods.summary: Graph f′ on the GDC; the inflexion of f is at a maximum or minimum of f′.

methods.name: Midpoint of a cubic's stationary points
methods.summary: A cubic's inflexion is midway between its two stationary points: here between x = 1 and x = 3.

misconceptions: Accepting f″ = 0 without a sign change: y = x⁴ has f″(0) = 0 but no inflexion
Substituting into f″ for the y-coordinate, giving (2, 0) instead of (2, 3)
Thinking an inflexion must have zero gradient (here f′(2) = −3)

threads.echo: A cubic has half-turn symmetry about its point of inflexion, which sits midway between its turning points.

skills.name: Interpret concavity and inflexion in context
examTypes: Find the time at which the population is growing fastest
Interpret the point of inflexion in context
Explain what f″(t) < 0 means for the sales of the product

methods.name: Inflexion as the extreme rate
methods.summary: The inflexion is where f′ is greatest or least, so 'growing fastest' means solve f″ = 0 (or find the maximum of f′).

methods.name: Read the bend of the graph
methods.summary: Concave down on a rising graph means it is still rising but more slowly; concave up means it is speeding up.

methods.name: GDC maximum of f′
methods.summary: Graph f′ and use the maximum tool to find the time of fastest growth.

misconceptions: Saying the population is decreasing because f″ < 0 (the growth rate is decreasing, not the population)
Placing the fastest growth at the maximum of P instead of at the point of inflexion
Reading the y-coordinate of the inflexion as the greatest rate instead of evaluating f′ there

threads.echo: Concavity is about how a rate changes: a rising graph that is concave down is still rising, just more slowly.

subtopics.title: Further integration: standard integrals, inspection and substitution
