subtopics.guide: Definite and indefinite integrals of xⁿ for rational n (including n = −1, giving ln x), sin x, cos x, 1/cos²x and eˣ. Integrating by inspection or by the substitution u = g(x) for integrals of the form ∫ f(g(x))g′(x) dx, including linear insides such as sin(2x + 5).

skills.name: Integrate the standard functions
examTypes: Find ∫ (3x² + 2/x + cos x) dx
Find ∫ 1/cos²x dx
Integrate 4√x − eˣ with respect to x

methods.name: Reverse the standard derivatives
methods.summary: xⁿ → xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) (n ≠ −1), 1/x → ln|x|, sin x → −cos x, cos x → sin x, 1/cos²x → tan x, eˣ → eˣ, each + C.

methods.name: Rewrite as powers
methods.summary: Write √x = x^(1/2) and 2/x = 2x⁻¹ before integrating.

methods.name: Differentiate to check
methods.summary: Differentiate your answer; you should get back the integrand.

misconceptions: ∫ sin x dx = cos x + C, losing the minus sign
Multiplying by the new power: ∫ √x dx = (3/2)x^(3/2) instead of (2/3)x^(3/2)
Using the power rule for 1/x, giving x⁰/0, instead of ln|x|
Leaving out + C on an indefinite integral

threads.echo: Integration undoes differentiation, so every standard integral is a standard derivative read backwards.
The + C says every antiderivative is a vertical translation of any other.

skills.name: Integrate a function of ax + b by inspection
examTypes: Find ∫ sin(2x + 5) dx
Find ∫ 1/(3x + 2) dx
Find ∫ e^(4x) dx

methods.name: Divide by the coefficient of x
methods.summary: Integrate the outer function and divide by a: ∫ sin(2x + 5) dx = −½cos(2x + 5) + C.

methods.name: Substitute u = ax + b
methods.summary: Let u = ax + b, du = a dx, integrate in u and substitute back.

methods.name: Differentiate to check
methods.summary: The chain rule on your answer must return the integrand exactly.

misconceptions: Multiplying by the inner coefficient: ∫ sin(2x + 5) dx = −2cos(2x + 5) + C
Missing the 1/3: ∫ 1/(3x + 2) dx = ln|3x + 2| + C instead of (1/3)ln|3x + 2| + C
Dividing by the whole exponent: ∫ e^(4x) dx = e^(4x)/(4x)

threads.echo: Dividing by a when integrating undoes the factor a the chain rule multiplies by when differentiating.

skills.name: Integrate ∫ f(g(x))g′(x) dx by substitution or inspection
examTypes: Find ∫ 4x sin(x²) dx
Use the substitution u = x² + 1 to find ∫ x(x² + 1)³ dx
Find ∫ sin x / cos x dx

methods.name: Substitute u = g(x)
methods.summary: Let u = x², du = 2x dx, so ∫ 4x sin(x²) dx = ∫ 2 sin u du = −2cos(x²) + C.

methods.name: Spot the reverse chain rule
methods.summary: Notice the derivative of the inside is a factor of the integrand and write the answer down, adjusting the constant: ∫ x(x² + 1)³ dx = (x² + 1)⁴/8 + C.

methods.name: Differentiate to check
methods.summary: Differentiate the answer with the chain rule to confirm.

misconceptions: Leaving dx unreplaced: writing ∫ 4x sin u dx and integrating 4x separately
Integrating the factors separately and multiplying: 2x² × (−cos(x²))
Losing the sign: ∫ sin x / cos x dx = ln|cos x| + C instead of −ln|cos x| + C

threads.echo: Substitution is the chain rule run backwards: the g′(x) factor is what the chain rule would have produced.

skills.name: Evaluate a definite integral exactly or with the GDC
examTypes: Find the exact value of ∫ from 0 to π/2 of cos x dx
Show that ∫ from 1 to e of 1/x dx = 1
Use your GDC to evaluate the integral

methods.name: Antiderivative, then F(b) − F(a)
methods.summary: Integrate, substitute the limits and subtract; with a substitution either change the limits to u or substitute back first.

methods.name: GDC integral
methods.summary: Use the GDC's definite integral function, in radian mode for trigonometric integrands.

misconceptions: Subtracting the wrong way round: F(a) − F(b)
Using degree mode: ∫ from 0 to π/2 of cos x dx comes out as about 1.57 instead of 1
Using the original x-limits after changing to u

threads.echo: A definite integral adds up f(x) × dx across the interval, giving a single number with no + C.

skills.name: Find a function from its derivative and a known point
examTypes: Given f′(x) = eˣ and f(0) = 5, find f(x)
The curve passes through (π, 2) and dy/dx = cos x + 2x. Find y
Find the equation of the curve given its gradient function

methods.name: Integrate, then find C
methods.summary: Integrate f′, substitute the known point and solve for C: f(x) = eˣ + C with f(0) = 5 gives C = 4.

methods.name: Add a definite integral
methods.summary: f(b) = f(a) + ∫ from a to b of f′(x) dx, evaluated on the GDC when only a value is needed.

misconceptions: Forgetting e⁰ = 1: taking C = 5 so f(x) = eˣ + 5
Leaving out C altogether and answering f(x) = eˣ
Substituting the point into f′ instead of into the integrated function

threads.echo: The known point picks out one curve from the family of vertical translations F(x) + C.
f(b) − f(a) is the total change, the accumulated sum of the rate f′ from a to b.

subtopics.title: Areas against either axis and volumes of revolution
subtopics.guide: Areas of regions bounded by a curve and either the x-axis or the y-axis over a given interval, including parts below the axis where the integral is negative. Volumes of revolution about the x-axis (V = ∫ πy² dx) or the y-axis (V = ∫ πx² dy).

skills.name: Find an area against the x-axis when part of the curve is below it
examTypes: Find the total area enclosed by the curve, the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 3
Explain why ∫ from 0 to 3 of f(x) dx is not the area
Write down an expression for the area of the shaded region

methods.name: Split at the x-intercepts
methods.summary: Find where the curve crosses the axis and integrate each piece; for y = x² − 4 on [0, 3] the pieces are −16/3 and 7/3, so the area is 16/3 + 7/3 = 23/3.

methods.name: Integrate |f(x)| on the GDC
methods.summary: Evaluate ∫ |f(x)| dx over the whole interval in one step.

misconceptions: Integrating straight across the root: ∫ from 0 to 3 of (x² − 4) dx = −3, so the area is given as 3 instead of 23/3
Giving a negative value (−16/3) as an area
Using the wrong x-intercept as a limit, e.g. −2 instead of 2

threads.echo: The integral adds signed pieces: strips below the axis count negatively, so an area needs each piece made positive.
Sketching the graph first shows where it crosses the axis and so where to split the integral.

skills.name: Find an area between a curve and the y-axis
examTypes: Find the area enclosed by the curve, the y-axis and the lines y = 0 and y = 4
Express x in terms of y and hence find the area
Write down an integral for the area of the region, in terms of y

methods.name: Rearrange and integrate x dy
methods.summary: Make x the subject and integrate with y-limits: for y = x², ∫ from 0 to 4 of √y dy = 16/3.

methods.name: Rectangle minus the x-axis area
methods.summary: Area to the y-axis = rectangle − area under the curve: 2 × 4 − 8/3 = 16/3.

methods.name: GDC integral in y
methods.summary: Enter x as a function of y and integrate between the y-limits on the GDC.

misconceptions: Integrating with respect to x but using y-limits: ∫ from 0 to 4 of x² dx = 64/3
Not rearranging: integrating ∫ y dy from 0 to 4 = 8
Using x-limits (0 to 2) in the y-integral

threads.echo: Swapping the roles of x and y turns an area against the y-axis into the familiar area under a curve.

skills.name: Find a volume of revolution about the x-axis
examTypes: The region under y = √x from x = 0 to x = 4 is rotated 360° about the x-axis. Find the volume
Write down an integral for the volume of the solid
Find the exact volume of the solid formed

methods.name: V = ∫ πy² dx
methods.summary: Square y, integrate with x-limits and multiply by π: π ∫ from 0 to 4 of x dx = 8π ≈ 25.1.

methods.name: GDC integral
methods.summary: Evaluate π ∫ y² dx on the GDC.

misconceptions: Not squaring y: π ∫ from 0 to 4 of √x dx = 16π/3
Leaving out π, giving 8
Squaring the integral of y instead of integrating y²

threads.echo: A volume of revolution adds up thin discs, each of volume πy² × dx.

skills.name: Find a volume of revolution about the y-axis
examTypes: The region between y = x², the y-axis and y = 4 is rotated about the y-axis. Find the volume
Express x² in terms of y and write down an integral for the volume
Find the volume of the bowl formed

methods.name: V = ∫ πx² dy
methods.summary: Make x² the subject in terms of y and integrate with y-limits: π ∫ from 0 to 4 of y dy = 8π.

methods.name: GDC integral in y
methods.summary: Enter x² as a function of y and integrate between the y-limits.

misconceptions: Using the x-axis formula: π ∫ from 0 to 2 of x⁴ dx = 32π/5
Using x-limits in the y-integral: π ∫ from 0 to 2 of y dy = 2π
Squaring y instead of x: π ∫ y² dy

threads.echo: Rotating about the y-axis stacks horizontal discs of area πx², added up through dy.

skills.name: Model a real object as a volume of revolution
examTypes: A vase is formed by rotating the curve about the y-axis. Find its capacity in litres
Find the depth of water when the bowl holds 500 cm³
Find the volume of material needed to make the solid

methods.name: GDC integral of the model
methods.summary: Set up π ∫ y² dx or π ∫ x² dy from the given curve and evaluate on the GDC.

methods.name: Solve for an unknown limit
methods.summary: Write V(h) = π ∫ from 0 to h of x² dy and solve V(h) = target with the GDC solver or graph intersection.

methods.name: Outer minus inner
methods.summary: For a hollow object, subtract the inner volume from the outer one.

misconceptions: Converting cm³ to litres by dividing by 100 instead of 1000
Rotating about the wrong axis for the shape described
Including the part of the curve outside the object's height

threads.echo: The capacity of a vase is the sum of many thin discs, each a small piece of the total volume.

subtopics.title: Setting up differential equations and separating variables
subtopics.guide: Forming a differential equation from a description in context, such as a rate proportional to the amount present, and solving it by separating the variables. Includes the general solution (with an arbitrary constant), particular solutions from given conditions, and the exponential model as the solution of dy/dx = ky.

skills.name: Write a differential equation from a description
examTypes: The rate of growth of the algae is proportional to the amount present. Write down a differential equation
A drink cools at a rate proportional to the difference between its temperature and the room temperature of 20 °C. Write down a differential equation
State the meaning of k in this model

methods.name: Translate the sentence
methods.summary: 'Rate of change of G' is dG/dt and 'proportional to' means = k × (…): dG/dt = kG.

methods.name: Check the sign
methods.summary: Decide whether the quantity grows or decays and give k or the expression the sign that matches: dT/dt = −k(T − 20) with k > 0.

misconceptions: Making the quantity, not its rate, proportional: G = kt instead of dG/dt = kG
Ignoring the surroundings: dT/dt = −kT instead of −k(T − 20)
Using a positive rate for a quantity that decays

threads.echo: A differential equation is a statement about a rate: how fast the quantity changes given where it is now.
'Rate proportional to amount' is the continuous version of multiplying by the same factor each step.

skills.name: Find the general solution by separating the variables
examTypes: Solve dy/dx = ky, giving the general solution
Find the general solution of dy/dx = xy
Use separation of variables to solve the differential equation

methods.name: Separate and integrate
methods.summary: Put all y terms with dy and all x terms with dx, integrate both sides with one + C, then rearrange: ∫ dy/y = ∫ k dx gives ln|y| = kx + C, so y = Ae^(kx).

methods.name: Recognise the exponential model
methods.summary: dy/dx = ky always has the solution y = Ae^(kx), so it can be written down and checked by differentiating.

misconceptions: Splitting the exponential: e^(kx + C) = e^(kx) + C, giving y = e^(kx) + C instead of Ae^(kx)
Integrating 1/y as y²/2 instead of ln|y|
Multiplying instead of separating, e.g. ∫ dy = ∫ xy dx with y treated as a constant

threads.echo: Separating dy/dx = ky lands on y = Ae^(kx): the solution is exponential growth or decay.
Taking exponentials undoes the ln that integration of 1/y produces.

skills.name: Find a particular solution and the constant k from data
examTypes: Given G = 200 when t = 0 and G = 350 when t = 3, find k
Find the particular solution that satisfies y(0) = 4
Find the value of the constant of integration

methods.name: Substitute and take logs
methods.summary: Use t = 0 for A, then the second value for k: 350 = 200e^(3k), so k = ln(1.75)/3 ≈ 0.187.

methods.name: GDC solver
methods.summary: Enter 200e^(3k) = 350 in the solver or intersect y = 200e^(3x) with y = 350.

misconceptions: Treating growth as linear: k = (350 − 200)/3 = 50
Substituting before finishing the rearrangement and then writing y = e^(kx) + C
Using ln(350/200) as k without dividing by 3

threads.echo: Two readings fix the growth factor: 350/200 over 3 time units gives e^(3k) = 1.75.

skills.name: Use the solution to predict and interpret
examTypes: Find the time at which the temperature reaches 40 °C
Describe what happens to G as t becomes large
Find the population after 10 years and comment on the model

methods.name: Solve with logarithms
methods.summary: Set the solution equal to the target value and take logs to find t.

methods.name: GDC intersection
methods.summary: Graph the solution and the target line and find the intersection.

methods.name: Long-term behaviour
methods.summary: As t → ∞, e^(−kt) → 0, so T = 20 + Ae^(−kt) tends to the room temperature 20 °C.

misconceptions: Predicting the temperature falls below the room temperature in the long run
Using the model far outside the data and accepting the answer without comment
Taking the log of each term separately: ln(20 + 60e^(−kt)) = ln 20 + ln 60 − kt

threads.echo: An exponential model keeps multiplying by the same factor, so it predicts unlimited growth, which a context may not allow.

skills.name: Show that a function is a solution of a differential equation
examTypes: Show that y = 3e^(2x) is a solution of dy/dx = 2y
Verify that T = 20 + 60e^(−0.1t) satisfies the differential equation
Explain why y = Ae^(kx) is called the general solution

methods.name: Differentiate and substitute
methods.summary: Find dy/dx from the proposed solution and check that both sides of the differential equation agree.

methods.name: Check at a point
methods.summary: Evaluate both sides numerically at one or two x-values on the GDC as a quick check.

misconceptions: Substituting a single x-value and calling it a proof
Checking the initial condition only, not the differential equation
Calling a particular solution such as y = 3e^(2x) the general solution

threads.echo: Differentiating the solution reverses the integration and should return the original equation.

subtopics.title: Slope fields
subtopics.guide: Using and interpreting slope fields for dy/dx = f(x, y): drawing short segments with the gradient at grid points, matching fields to equations, sketching solution curves through a given point and reading features such as equilibrium solutions and long-term behaviour.

skills.name: Draw slope-field segments at given points
examTypes: Complete the slope field for dy/dx = x − y at the points shown
Find the gradient of the segment at (2, 1)
Draw the segments at the grid points where x = 0

methods.name: Evaluate at each point
methods.summary: Substitute each (x, y) into the equation to get the gradient and draw a short segment with that slope: for dy/dx = x − y, (2, 0) gives 2.

methods.name: Use lines of equal slope
methods.summary: Every point on x − y = c has the same slope c, so draw whole lines of parallel segments at once.

misconceptions: Swapping the coordinates: at (2, 0) drawing slope 0 − 2 = −2 instead of 2
Drawing a slope-0 segment vertically instead of horizontally
Drawing segments as long arrows that join up across grid points

threads.echo: Each segment is a tiny tangent: the differential equation gives the gradient at that point.

skills.name: Match a slope field to its differential equation
examTypes: Which slope field belongs to dy/dx = y?
Match each differential equation to its slope field
Explain why the field cannot be for dy/dx = x²

methods.name: Look for row or column patterns
methods.summary: If dy/dx depends only on x, the segments are identical down each vertical column; if only on y, identical along each horizontal row.

methods.name: Test a few points
methods.summary: Compare the equations at points where they differ, e.g. the sign of the slope at (1, −1).

misconceptions: Mixing up the patterns: thinking dy/dx = y gives identical columns
Testing only (0, 0), where several equations all give slope 0
Ignoring signs: matching dy/dx = −x to the field of dy/dx = x

threads.echo: A field that depends only on x looks the same after any vertical shift, so every solution curve is a vertical translation of another.

skills.name: Sketch a solution curve through a given point
examTypes: On the slope field, sketch the solution curve that passes through (0, 1)
Use the slope field to estimate y when x = 2 for this solution
Sketch the particular solution with y(0) = −1

methods.name: Follow the segments
methods.summary: Start at the given point and draw a smooth curve that is tangent to the nearby segments, in both directions.

methods.name: Use where the slope is zero
methods.summary: Where the curve crosses the zero-slope isocline it is momentarily flat, giving its maximum or minimum.

misconceptions: Drawing the curve across the segments instead of along them
Sketching only to the right of the given point
Joining separate segments with straight lines, giving a jagged path

threads.echo: A solution curve can be sketched from the field even when the equation cannot be solved algebraically.

skills.name: Read equilibria and long-term behaviour from a slope field
examTypes: Write down the equation of the equilibrium solution
Describe what happens to y as x increases for a solution starting at y = 1
State whether the equilibrium is stable

methods.name: Solve dy/dx = 0 for all x
methods.summary: Equilibrium solutions are horizontal lines y = c where the rate is 0 for every x: dy/dx = y(3 − y) gives y = 0 and y = 3.

methods.name: Read the direction of nearby segments
methods.summary: If nearby solutions head towards the line from both sides it is stable; if they move away it is unstable.

misconceptions: Treating points where a curve crosses the x-axis as equilibria
Calling y = 0 stable for dy/dx = y(3 − y), when solutions move away from it
Thinking the slope is zero at every point of an isocline other than the zero one

threads.echo: Where a solution curve meets the zero-slope isocline it has a turning point, the slope-field version of f′(x) = 0.

subtopics.title: Euler's method for single and coupled first-order equations
subtopics.guide: Euler's method for approximate solutions of dy/dx = f(x, y) and of coupled systems dx/dt = f₁(x, y, t), dy/dt = f₂(x, y, t), such as predator-prey models. Values are generated with a spreadsheet or GDC; students should understand the step-by-step method, the effect of the step size and how to interpret the output.

skills.name: Apply a few steps of Euler's method
examTypes: Use Euler's method with h = 0.1 to find y₁ and y₂
Write down the formula for yₙ₊₁
Complete the table of Euler's method values

methods.name: yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h f(xₙ, yₙ)
methods.summary: Evaluate the gradient at the current point, step along it, then update x: dy/dx = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1 gives y₁ = 1.1, y₂ = 1.22.

methods.name: Table of steps
methods.summary: Lay out columns n, xₙ, yₙ, f(xₙ, yₙ), h·f and fill row by row.

misconceptions: Using the new x with the old y: y₂ = 1.1 + 0.1(0.2 + 1.1) = 1.23 instead of 1.22
Forgetting to multiply by h: y₁ = 1 + 1 = 2
Taking 4 steps of h = 0.1 to reach x = 0.5

threads.echo: Each Euler step uses the gradient at the current point as if it stayed constant over a short step.
Each step moves from (xₙ, yₙ) by the vector (h, h·f(xₙ, yₙ)), a short walk along the tangent.

skills.name: Use a spreadsheet or GDC for many Euler steps
examTypes: Use Euler's method with h = 0.05 to estimate y when x = 2
Write down the value of y after 20 steps
Find the first value of x for which the estimate of y exceeds 10

methods.name: Spreadsheet columns
methods.summary: Set up columns for x and y with the update formulas and fill down to the required x.

methods.name: GDC sequence mode or program
methods.summary: Use recursive sequences or a short program for xₙ and yₙ and read the required row.

misconceptions: Reading the row one step early or late (off by one)
Rounding each intermediate value to 3 s.f., so the final answer drifts
Using the wrong number of steps: (b − a)/h computed incorrectly

threads.echo: The Euler estimate is the starting value plus the sum of many small changes h·f, a running total.

skills.name: Apply Euler's method to a coupled system
examTypes: Use Euler's method with h = 0.1 to estimate the numbers of prey and predators after one step
Write down the update formulas for xₙ₊₁ and yₙ₊₁
Estimate both populations when t = 5

methods.name: Update both from the old values
methods.summary: xₙ₊₁ = xₙ + h f₁(xₙ, yₙ, tₙ), yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h f₂(xₙ, yₙ, tₙ), tₙ₊₁ = tₙ + h; for dx/dt = 0.5x − 0.01xy, dy/dt = −0.4y + 0.005xy from (100, 20) with h = 0.1 this gives (103, 20.2).

methods.name: Spreadsheet with three columns
methods.summary: Columns for t, x and y, each new row computed from the previous row only.

misconceptions: Using the new x in the y update: y₁ = 20 + 0.1(−8 + 0.005 × 103 × 20) = 20.23 instead of 20.2
Using different step sizes for x and y
Forgetting to update t when f₁ or f₂ depends on t

threads.echo: Each step moves the point (x, y) by h times the rate vector (f₁, f₂).

skills.name: Judge the accuracy of an Euler approximation
examTypes: Explain how the accuracy could be improved
Find the percentage error compared with the exact solution
State, with a reason, whether Euler's method overestimates or underestimates here

methods.name: Halve the step size
methods.summary: Repeat with a smaller h and see the estimate settle; smaller steps give a better approximation.

methods.name: Tangent above or below the curve
methods.summary: If the solution curve is concave up, each tangent step lies below the curve, so Euler underestimates; concave down gives an overestimate.

methods.name: Compare with the exact solution
methods.summary: Where the equation can be solved by separating variables, find the exact value and the percentage error.

misconceptions: Thinking a larger step is more accurate because there are fewer steps
Reversing the concavity rule: saying Euler overestimates a concave-up solution
Expecting a small enough step to give the exact answer

threads.echo: Euler treats the rate as constant over each step; the more the rate changes within a step, the bigger the error.

skills.name: Interpret a coupled model and its equilibrium
examTypes: Explain the meaning of the term −0.01xy in context
Find the non-zero equilibrium populations
Describe how the populations change over time from the Euler output

methods.name: Set both rates to zero
methods.summary: Solve f₁ = 0 and f₂ = 0 together: 0.5x − 0.01xy = 0 and −0.4y + 0.005xy = 0 give (80, 50) as well as (0, 0).

methods.name: Read the technology output
methods.summary: Plot x and y against t, or y against x, from the Euler values and describe the cycle or trend.

misconceptions: Setting only one rate to zero and calling that an equilibrium
Reading the xy term in the prey equation as helping the prey
Swapping the equilibrium values, giving (50, 80)

threads.echo: At an equilibrium both rates are zero at once, so neither population rises or falls.

subtopics.title: Phase portraits for coupled linear differential equations
subtopics.guide: Phase portraits for dx/dt = ax + by, dy/dt = cx + dy with distinct non-zero eigenvalues: classifying the origin from the eigenvalues (real, complex or purely imaginary), sketching trajectories and identifying equilibrium points, stability and saddle points. Exact solutions are only needed for real distinct eigenvalues.

skills.name: Classify the behaviour from the eigenvalues
examTypes: Find the eigenvalues of the matrix and describe the behaviour of solutions near the origin
Show that the origin is a saddle point
State whether solutions spiral towards or away from the origin

methods.name: Solve the characteristic equation
methods.summary: Solve λ² − (a + d)λ + (ad − bc) = 0; dx/dt = x + 2y, dy/dt = 2x + y gives λ = 3 and −1, a saddle.

methods.name: GDC eigenvalues
methods.summary: Enter the matrix and use the eigenvalue function.

methods.name: Trace and determinant
methods.summary: det < 0 gives a saddle; with det > 0, a negative trace means solutions approach the origin, a positive trace that they move away, and trace 0 gives closed orbits.

misconceptions: Calling a saddle stable because one eigenvalue is negative
Calling purely imaginary eigenvalues (±2i) a spiral instead of closed ellipses
Judging −1 ± 2i as moving away because the imaginary part is positive (the negative real part decides: towards the origin)

threads.echo: The eigenvectors are the directions along which the motion is a pure stretch, so the eigenvalues say whether paths grow or shrink.

skills.name: Write the exact solution for real distinct eigenvalues
examTypes: Find the general solution of the system
Given x = 3 and y = 1 when t = 0, find the particular solution
Write down the solution in terms of eigenvectors

methods.name: Eigenvector form
methods.summary: Write (x, y) = Ae^(λ₁t)v₁ + Be^(λ₂t)v₂; for λ = 3, v = (1, 1) and λ = −1, v = (1, −1), the start (3, 1) gives A = 2, B = 1.

methods.name: GDC eigenvectors and solver
methods.summary: Find the eigenvectors on the GDC, then solve for A and B from the initial values.

misconceptions: Pairing each eigenvalue with the wrong eigenvector: Ae^(3t)(1, −1) + Be^(−t)(1, 1)
Taking A and B as the initial values x(0) and y(0) directly
Writing e^(λ)·t instead of e^(λt)

threads.echo: Along each eigenvector the solution grows or decays exponentially like e^(λt).

skills.name: Sketch trajectories on a phase portrait
examTypes: Sketch the phase portrait, showing the eigenvector directions
Sketch the trajectory that starts at (1, 0)
Determine whether the trajectories rotate clockwise or anticlockwise

methods.name: Draw the eigenvector lines
methods.summary: Draw the straight-line solutions along each eigenvector, arrows outward for positive eigenvalues and inward for negative ones, and curve other paths between them.

methods.name: Velocity at test points
methods.summary: Evaluate (dx/dt, dy/dt) at points such as (1, 0): if dy/dt = c > 0 there, the rotation is anticlockwise.

methods.name: Use the lines dx/dt = 0 and dy/dt = 0
methods.summary: Paths cross dx/dt = 0 vertically and dy/dt = 0 horizontally, which fixes their shape.

misconceptions: Drawing arrows towards the origin along the eigenvector of the positive eigenvalue
Guessing the direction of rotation instead of checking the velocity at a point
Drawing trajectories that cross each other

threads.echo: At every point the system gives a velocity vector (dx/dt, dy/dt), and a trajectory follows these arrows.

skills.name: Interpret equilibrium, stability and long-term behaviour
examTypes: Describe the long-term behaviour of the populations starting from (3, 1)
Explain why the origin is unstable
State the ratio y : x in the long term

methods.name: Find the dominant term
methods.summary: As t grows, the term with the largest eigenvalue dominates: with 2e^(3t)(1, 1) + e^(−t)(1, −1), the path approaches the direction (1, 1), so y : x → 1.

methods.name: Read the phase portrait
methods.summary: Follow the trajectory from the starting point and see where it heads: to the origin, away from it, round it, or out along an eigenvector.

misconceptions: Assuming every path approaches the origin in a saddle (only those starting on the stable eigenvector line do)
Saying solutions with imaginary eigenvalues settle at the origin instead of cycling
Taking the eigenvector of the smaller eigenvalue as the long-term direction

threads.echo: The fastest exponential term eventually swamps the others, so the largest eigenvalue decides the long-term direction.

subtopics.title: Second-order differential equations by Euler's method
subtopics.guide: Approximate solutions of second-order equations d²x/dt² = f(x, dx/dt, t) by rewriting them as the coupled system dx/dt = y, dy/dt = f(x, y, t) and applying Euler's method. Equations of the form d²x/dt² + a dx/dt + bx = 0 can also be studied with the phase portraits of AHL5.17; the equation is always given in examinations.

skills.name: Rewrite a second-order equation as two first-order equations
examTypes: Write the equation as a system of two first-order differential equations
Write down the initial value of y
Write the system in matrix form

methods.name: Let y = dx/dt
methods.summary: Set dx/dt = y, so d²x/dt² = dy/dt and solve the equation for it: x″ + 3x′ + 2x = 0 gives dy/dt = −2x − 3y, with y(0) = x′(0).

misconceptions: Not moving the terms across: dy/dt = 2x + 3y instead of −2x − 3y
Swapping the coefficients: dy/dt = −3x − 2y
Using x(0) as the initial value of y instead of x′(0)

threads.echo: A second-order equation and the pair dx/dt = y, dy/dt = f(x, y, t) say the same thing in a form Euler's method can use.

skills.name: Approximate a second-order solution with Euler's method
examTypes: Use Euler's method with h = 0.1 to estimate x when t = 1
Find x₂ and y₂
Estimate the velocity after 0.5 seconds

methods.name: Spreadsheet or GDC
methods.summary: Set up columns t, x, y with the update formulas and fill down to the required time.

misconceptions: Updating x with the new y: x₁ = 1 + 0.1(−0.4) = 0.96 at the first step instead of 1
Giving the y column (velocity) when x is asked for
Applying Euler to x″ directly as xₙ₊₁ = xₙ + h f, skipping the velocity

threads.echo: Each step moves the state (x, y) by h times the vector (y, f(x, y, t)).

skills.name: Classify x″ + ax′ + bx = 0 with eigenvalues and phase portraits
examTypes: Write the system in matrix form and find the eigenvalues
Describe the phase portrait for x″ + 2x′ + 5x = 0
Explain whether the motion is oscillatory

methods.name: Matrix and characteristic equation
methods.summary: The matrix is (0, 1; −b, −a), with characteristic equation λ² + aλ + b = 0: x″ + 2x′ + 5x = 0 gives λ = −1 ± 2i, spiralling into the origin.

methods.name: GDC eigenvalues
methods.summary: Enter the matrix (0, 1; −b, −a) and find the eigenvalues on the GDC.

misconceptions: Using λ² − aλ + b: for x″ + 2x′ + 5x = 0 this gives 1 ± 2i and wrongly predicts spiralling outwards
Putting −a and −b in the wrong places in the matrix
Describing x″ + 4x = 0 (λ = ±2i) as a spiral instead of closed ellipses

threads.echo: The same equation can be read as one second-order equation or as a 2 × 2 matrix system, and the eigenvalues of the matrix are the roots of λ² + aλ + b = 0.

skills.name: Interpret a second-order model in context
examTypes: Describe the motion of the spring as t increases
Use the Euler values to find when the object first passes through the equilibrium position
Interpret a spiral phase portrait in terms of the motion

methods.name: Read the Euler table
methods.summary: Look for the first sign change in the x column for passing through equilibrium, or the largest |x| for the greatest displacement.

methods.name: Read the phase portrait
methods.summary: With x as displacement and y as velocity, a spiral into the origin is a damped oscillation and a closed loop an undamped one.

misconceptions: Reading the y column as the displacement
Thinking a spiral phase portrait means the object moves in a circle in space
Calling a stable node an oscillation (it returns to equilibrium without oscillating)

threads.echo: The greatest displacement happens where the velocity y is zero, where a trajectory crosses the x-axis of the phase plane.
